conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Usually a low-energy fall in an elderly (osteoporotic) patient — a fragility fracture; in the young it requires high-energy trauma.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What does X-ray show in a neck of femur fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The fracture on AP + lateral views; an intracapsular fracture disrupts Shenton's line (the smooth curve along the inferior femoral neck and superior pubic ramus).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is Shenton's line, and what does its disruption indicate?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A smooth curve along the inferior femoral neck and superior pubic ramus; a break in it indicates a fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What imaging is used if the X-ray is normal but a hip fracture is clinically suspected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: MRI (most sensitive) — or CT — to detect an occult fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What pre-operative workup is needed for a hip fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Bloods, ECG, group & save, fitness for anaesthesia; plus assessment/treatment of the osteoporosis (DEXA) and a falls assessment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the management principle for a neck of femur fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Surgery for almost all (early — within 36–48h); the operation is chosen by intracapsular-vs-extracapsular and displaced-vs-undisplaced (driven by AVN risk); plus analgesia and treating the osteoporosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is an UNDISPLACED intracapsular fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Internal fixation (blood supply usually preserved); a hemiarthroplasty if the patient is unfit.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a DISPLACED intracapsular fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Arthroplasty — THR or hemiarthroplasty — because the retrograde supply is disrupted (AVN risk → must replace).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: When is a THR favoured over a hemiarthroplasty for a displaced intracapsular fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: When the patient (all of): was able to walk independently outdoors with no more than a stick; is not cognitively impaired; and is medically fit for anaesthesia and the procedure. Frailer patients get a hemiarthroplasty.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a STABLE intertrochanteric (extracapsular) fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A dynamic hip screw (DHS).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a reverse oblique/transverse/subtrochanteric (extracapsular) fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: An intramedullary nail.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: When should surgery ideally occur for a hip fracture, and when can the patient weight-bear?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Early — within ~36–48 hours; the patient should weight-bear immediately after the operation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What supportive/orthogeriatric measures accompany hip fracture surgery?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Adequate analgesia (± fascia iliaca block), orthogeriatric care, early mobilisation, treating the osteoporosis (Ca/vit D + bisphosphonate), a falls assessment, VTE prophylaxis, delirium prevention, pressure care and nutrition.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Why does a hip fragility fracture mandate osteoporosis treatment and a falls assessment?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: It is a fragility fracture, so treating the osteoporosis and addressing falls risk helps prevent the next fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a patellar fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A fracture of the patella (kneecap) — the sesamoid within the quadriceps/patellar tendon that acts as the fulcrum for knee extension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the 'core concept' of a patellar fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The patella is the linchpin of the extensor mechanism (quadriceps → patella → patellar tendon → tibial tuberosity), so the single most important question is whether the extensor mechanism is intact — can the patient straight-leg raise / actively extend the knee?

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What single clinical test drives the management of a patellar fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Active knee extension / straight-leg raise — intact + undisplaced → conservative (brace); disrupted or displaced → surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How does a DIRECT injury tend to fracture the patella?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A blow to the front of the knee → an undisplaced crack OR a comminuted fracture, with the extensor mechanism usually INTACT.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How does an INDIRECT injury fracture the patella?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A violent quadriceps contraction against a block to extension → a TRANSVERSE fracture that pulls apart, which can DISRUPT the extensor mechanism.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the clinical features of a patellar fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Anterior knee pain, swelling and bruising with tenderness localised to the patella after trauma; a palpable gap/defect over the patella (in a displaced transverse fracture); and a haemarthrosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What does a palpable gap/defect over the patella suggest?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A displaced transverse fracture with a disrupted extensor mechanism.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How do you assess the extensor mechanism in a patellar fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Ask whether the patient can actively extend the knee / straight-leg raise — if they CAN, the mechanism is INTACT; if they CANNOT, it is DISRUPTED (needs surgery).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the technique tip for testing the extensor mechanism, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Test on the patient's SIDE to eliminate gravity — removing gravity's resistance means pain doesn't cause a false 'can't lift'.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What imaging is used for a patellar fracture, and which view is most useful?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Plain X-ray (AP + lateral) confirms the fracture and assesses displacement/pattern (transverse/comminuted); the lateral view best shows displacement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a bipartite patella, and why does it matter?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A normal variant — a smooth, superolateral separate ossicle (often bilateral, with smooth margins); it must not be mistaken for a fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the management of an undisplaced patellar fracture with an intact extensor mechanism?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: No surgery — a hinged knee brace for 6 weeks, and the patient can fully weight-bear.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the management of a displaced patellar fracture or one with a lost extensor mechanism?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Surgery — tension band wire, inter-fragment screws or cerclage wires — followed by a hinged brace for 4–6 weeks.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the classic fixation for a transverse patellar fracture, and how does it work?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Tension band wiring — it converts the distracting tensile forces of the quadriceps into compressive forces across the fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What supportive measures accompany patellar fracture management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Analgesia, physiotherapy (regain quadriceps strength and range) and early mobilisation in the brace.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is done for severe comminution of the patella?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Partial or total patellectomy (rarely).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Can a patient with an undisplaced patellar fracture and intact extensor mechanism weight-bear?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Yes — they can fully weight-bear (in a hinged knee brace).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Summarise the decisive fork in patellar fracture management.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Intact extensor mechanism + undisplaced → conservative (hinged brace); disrupted mechanism or displaced → surgical fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is an ankle fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A fracture of the malleoli (± the distal tibia/fibula) around the ankle joint — one of the commonest lower-limb fractures, usually from a twisting/inversion injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the 'core concept' of ankle fractures (the mortise)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The ankle is a 'mortise' — a socket of distal tibia + medial malleolus + lateral malleolus (fibula), held by the syndesmosis; mortise stability is everything.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What two questions organise ankle fracture assessment?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: (1) Is it fractured? (use the Ottawa ankle rules to decide who needs an X-ray); and (2) is it STABLE? (the Weber classification, based on where the fibular fracture sits relative to the syndesmosis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the overall flow for managing an ankle injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Ottawa (do I image?) → Weber (is it stable?) → treat (stable → conservative boot; unstable → surgery/ORIF).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the Weber classification?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Weber A = fibular fracture BELOW the syndesmosis (syndesmosis intact → stable); Weber B = at the tibial plafond/syndesmosis level (variable — check stability); Weber C = ABOVE the syndesmosis (syndesmosis disrupted → unstable).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How does fibular fracture height relate to ankle stability in the Weber system?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The higher the fibular fracture, the more likely the syndesmosis is disrupted and the ankle unstable (disrupted syndesmosis → unstable mortise → surgery).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the Ottawa ankle rules?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: An X-ray is needed only if there is malleolar-zone pain AND any of: inability to weight-bear for 4 steps (immediately and in the department); bony tenderness over the distal tibia (posterior edge/tip of the medial malleolus); or bony tenderness over the distal fibula (posterior edge/tip of the lateral malleolus).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the purpose of the Ottawa ankle rules?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: To minimise unnecessary X-rays — a negative assessment makes a fracture unlikely.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the Ottawa FOOT rules for?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Midfoot-zone pain — an X-ray if there is bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular (or inability to weight-bear).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the typical mechanism of an ankle fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A twisting/inversion (or eversion) injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the clinical features of an ankle fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Pain, swelling, bruising, deformity, inability to weight-bear and malleolar tenderness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What must be assessed on examination of an ankle fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The skin (tented/threatened — a deformed/dislocated ankle risks necrosis → prompt reduction); neurovascular status (pulses, sensation, capillary refill, before + after reduction); and the whole fibula.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a Maisonneuve fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A proximal fibular fracture with a syndesmosis injury — so always check the whole fibula in an ankle injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What X-ray views are used for an ankle fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: AP, lateral and mortise views — to assess the fracture, the Weber type, and mortise congruity/syndesmosis (CT for complex/comminuted fractures or surgical planning).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Why does a Weber B fracture specifically need a radiograph (± stress/weight-bearing views)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: To check the syndesmosis and mortise for stability, as Weber B fractures can be stable or unstable.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the critical safety rule regarding reduction and X-rays in ankle fractures?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Do NOT delay for an X-ray in an obvious ankle injury with neurovascular compromise → REDUCE FIRST.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Why should ALL deformed/dislocated ankle fractures be promptly reduced?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: To remove pressure on the overlying skin and prevent necrosis (closed reduction is the most immediate management).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a Weber A ankle fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A CAM boot with weight-bearing as tolerated (it is stable).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a Weber B ankle fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Radiograph to check the syndesmosis + mortise: if stable → CAM boot; if unstable (ligaments affected) → surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a Weber C ankle fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: ORIF (the syndesmosis is disrupted → unstable), often with a compression plate and syndesmotic screw/fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which ankle fractures usually need surgical repair?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Young patients, and unstable/high-velocity/proximal injuries — often with a compression plate; a disrupted syndesmosis needs stabilisation (syndesmotic screw/fixation).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What supportive measures accompany ankle fracture management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Analgesia, elevation, RICE, physiotherapy, and VTE prophylaxis if immobilised.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are metatarsal fractures?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Fractures of the long bones of the forefoot — the commonest foot fractures, with the 5th metatarsal most commonly fractured and the 2nd metatarsal the classic stress-fracture site.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What two patterns dominate metatarsal fractures?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: (1) The 5th metatarsal base — where the critical distinction is a proximal avulsion (pseudo-Jones) vs a true Jones fracture (different zones/blood supplies/healing); and (2) the stress fracture — a fatigue fracture from repetitive loading in athletes, classically the 2nd metatarsal shaft.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a pseudo-Jones fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: An AVULSION of the proximal tuberosity of the 5th metatarsal from an inversion injury/lateral ankle sprain — the most common 5th metatarsal fracture, with a good blood supply so it heals well.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a Jones fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A transverse fracture of the 5th metatarsal at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction — less common, at a watershed zone with a poorer blood supply → risk of non-union/delayed union.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How do pseudo-Jones and Jones fractures differ in location and healing?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Pseudo-Jones = proximal tuberosity avulsion, good blood supply → heals well (usually conservative); Jones = transverse at the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction, watershed zone → poorer healing/non-union risk (closer follow-up ± surgery).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What mechanism causes a pseudo-Jones fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A lateral ankle sprain — an inversion injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Why should you 'examine the foot, not just the ankle' after an inversion injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A 'sprained ankle' can actually be a 5th metatarsal base fracture, so examine the foot as well as the ankle.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which metatarsal is most commonly affected by a STRESS (fatigue) fracture, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The 2nd metatarsal shaft — it is longer and thinner (a 'march fracture').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the mechanism and typical patient of a metatarsal stress fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Repetitive loading in an otherwise healthy athlete, giving gradual, insidious, activity-related forefoot pain worse with loading and eased by rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How does an acute traumatic metatarsal fracture differ from a stress fracture in site and onset?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Acute: 5th metatarsal base, sudden onset (inversion/direct blow/twist), usually visible on X-ray. Stress: 2nd metatarsal shaft, gradual/insidious onset, X-ray often normal early.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the clinical features of a metatarsal fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Forefoot pain, bony tenderness, swelling and an antalgic gait (limping to avoid forefoot loading).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What imaging is first-line for a metatarsal fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: X-ray (AP, lateral, oblique) — to differentiate displaced from non-displaced and show acute fractures (e.g. a Jones fracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a suspected stress fracture with a normal early X-ray investigated?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: With MRI (most sensitive) or an isotope bone scan (shows increased uptake); a repeat X-ray at ~2 weeks may show healing callus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the Ottawa foot rules for?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Midfoot-zone pain — an X-ray if there is bony tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to weight-bear.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the general management of most (undisplaced) metatarsal fractures?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Conservative — stiff-soled/supportive footwear or a walking boot/cast, weight-bear as tolerated, analgesia and elevation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a pseudo-Jones (5th metatarsal avulsion) fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Usually conservatively — supportive footwear/boot, weight-bear as tolerated (it heals well).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a Jones fracture managed, and why more cautiously?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: More cautiously because of the non-union risk (watershed zone): immobilisation + non-weight-bearing with closer follow-up, and surgical fixation (screw) considered, especially in athletes or if it fails to unite.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a metatarsal stress fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Rest + activity modification with a gradual/graded return, and treating any underlying cause (training errors, biomechanics, low bone density/energy availability).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How are displaced/multiple/unstable metatarsal fractures managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Reduction ± surgical fixation (ORIF/K-wires).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Summarise the management fork for metatarsal fractures.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Undisplaced → conservative (boot, weight-bear as tolerated); Jones fracture → cautious ± surgery (non-union risk); stress fracture → rest + graded return; displaced/multiple → fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A fracture of the proximal tibial articular surface (the plateau) — the weight-bearing top of the tibia that forms the lower half of the knee joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the 'core concept' of a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: It is an intra-articular, weight-bearing surface, so it matters for two reasons: (1) joint congruity — any step-off/depression predisposes to post-traumatic osteoarthritis; and (2) associated soft-tissue/neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome from the mechanism.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which tibial plateau is most commonly fractured, and by what force?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The lateral plateau — from a valgus force.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the classic mechanism of a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A high-energy axial load (fall from height, road traffic accident / 'bumper injury') or a low-energy fall in the osteoporotic elderly — axial load ± valgus/varus force to the knee.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is a lipohaemarthrosis, and what does it signify?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Aspirating blood with fat globules (or a fat-fluid level on imaging) — marrow fat leaking into the joint — indicating an intra-articular fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which neurovascular structures are at risk in a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: The popliteal artery and the common peroneal nerve — assess distal pulses ± ABPI and the peroneal nerve/foot drop.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Why are proximal tibial fractures a classic cause of compartment syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Swelling in the proximal leg compartments — watch for pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the clinical features of a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A painful, swollen knee (often a large/tense haemarthrosis), inability to weight-bear, restricted movement and ± deformity, after axial trauma.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What must always be assessed in a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Neurovascular status (popliteal artery, common peroneal nerve), compartment syndrome, the skin (open fracture?), and associated ligament/meniscal injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How do high-energy and low-energy tibial plateau fractures differ?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: High-energy (young): road traffic accident/bumper injury/fall from height/sport → complex, comminuted, displaced, bicondylar, high associated injury. Low-energy (elderly osteoporotic): simple fall → simple depression/split, lower associated injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the first-line imaging for a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: X-ray (AP + lateral) — shows the fracture, articular depression/split and a lipohaemarthrosis (fat-fluid level).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the KEY investigation for a tibial plateau fracture, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: CT — it defines the articular surface (depression/step-off + comminution) for surgical planning, essential for most plateau fractures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: When are MRI and CT angiography used in a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: MRI for associated ligament + meniscal injuries (± occult fractures); CT angiography if vascular injury is suspected (especially with a dislocation component).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the Schatzker classification, grades I–VI?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: I = lateral split (young, dense bone); II = lateral split + depression (the commonest); III = lateral depression only (elderly, osteoporotic); IV = medial plateau (higher-energy, ↑ neurovascular risk); V = bicondylar (both plateaus); VI = plateau fracture with metaphyseal–diaphyseal dissociation (highest energy).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which is the commonest Schatzker type?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Schatzker II — a lateral split + depression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: Which Schatzker types carry the highest neurovascular/compartment risk?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Schatzker IV–VI (medial/bicondylar and metaphyseal–diaphyseal dissociation) — higher number = higher energy, more complex, more associated injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the management principle for a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Restore the articular surface + knee alignment/stability; undisplaced → conservative; displaced/depressed intra-articular → ORIF; manage the associated emergencies (compartment syndrome/vascular injury) first.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the immediate steps in a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: ABCDE (if high-energy), analgesia, assess and document neurovascular status + compartment syndrome, splint; an open fracture → antibiotics + urgent debridement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is an UNDISPLACED (stable, minimal depression) tibial plateau fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: A hinged knee brace + protected/non-weight-bearing, then graded weight-bearing and physiotherapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How is a DISPLACED/depressed intra-articular tibial plateau fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: ORIF — elevate the depressed fragment, bone graft the defect, and stabilise with plates/screws to restore a congruent joint surface.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: How are associated injuries managed in a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Compartment syndrome → fasciotomy; vascular injury → revascularisation; ligament/meniscal repair as needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What is the KEY long-term complication of a tibial plateau fracture, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Post-traumatic osteoarthritis — from articular incongruity (hence the emphasis on restoring the joint surface).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.front: What are the key ACUTE complications of a tibial plateau fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.back: Compartment syndrome and neurovascular injury (popliteal artery, peroneal nerve).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the organising principle for lower back & spine problems?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Most back pain is mechanical and self-limiting — the skill is screening for red flags (cauda equina, malignancy, infection, fracture) and recognising radicular features.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the classic clues for each major cause of back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Mechanical LBP = activity-related, no red flags; sciatica/prolapsed disc = radicular dermatomal leg pain with positive straight-leg raise; spinal stenosis = neurogenic claudication (leg pain on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting); discitis = infective (fever, focal tenderness, raised inflammatory markers); osteoporotic vertebral fracture = acute pain after minor stress in an older/osteoporotic patient.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What features screen for cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica → urgent MRI + surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: List the red flags for back pain.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Age <20 or >50, weight loss, night pain, fever, trauma, a history of cancer, and saddle anaesthesia/bladder-bowel dysfunction (cauda equina).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is mechanical (non-specific) lower back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Back pain from the muscles, ligaments, joints or discs of the spine without a serious underlying cause — the commonest cause of back pain by far (>90%).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'core concept' of mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: The overwhelming majority of back pain is benign, self-limiting and 'mechanical', so the task is NOT to image everyone but to screen for the red flags signalling a serious cause (cancer, infection, fracture, cauda equina).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What features characterise BENIGN mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Pain that varies with posture/movement, no systemic features, improvement with rest/activity, no neurological deficit, and a self-limiting course.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which red-flag features point to MALIGNANCY / metastatic spinal cord compression?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Age >50, previous cancer, night pain and weight loss.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which red-flag features point to spinal INFECTION (discitis/epidural abscess)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Fever, being systemically unwell, and IV drug use.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which red-flag features point to a vertebral FRACTURE?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Trauma, osteoporosis and steroid use.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What combination indicates cauda equina syndrome, and what is the action?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Saddle anaesthesia + urinary retention/incontinence + faecal incontinence + bilateral sciatica = cauda equina syndrome → EMERGENCY MRI + decompression (the 'must-never-miss').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the causes of mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Non-specific/mechanical (muscle/ligament strain, poor posture, lifting) — commonest; degenerative (facet joint OA, degenerative disc disease, spondylosis); discogenic/radiculopathy (prolapsed disc → sciatica); lumbar spinal stenosis; and spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the mechanical pain pattern?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Pain in the lower back (± buttock/thigh), worse with movement/certain postures, better with rest, no systemic features, and no true morning stiffness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is sciatica, in terms of clinical pattern?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Pain radiating down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern (± paraesthesia/weakness) — from nerve root compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How does an INFLAMMATORY back pain pattern differ from mechanical, and what should it prompt?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Inflammatory = morning stiffness, better with movement, in a young patient → think ankylosing spondylitis (not mechanical).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Should mechanical back pain be routinely imaged?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: No — do NOT routinely image mechanical back pain; MRI is reserved for red flags/suspected serious pathology, radiculopathy not settling, or before intervention (routine X-rays/MRI are unhelpful — radiation, incidental findings).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: When is URGENT MRI indicated in back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Suspected cauda equina, cord compression (malignancy), or infection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What blood tests are done if infection or malignancy is suspected in back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: FBC, CRP/ESR, ± a myeloma screen / PSA.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the management principle for benign mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Reassurance + education (most is benign and self-limiting), stay active and continue normal activities (avoid bed rest, which worsens outcomes), and analgesia — with red-flag conditions getting urgent referral/specific treatment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the first-line analgesia for mechanical back pain per NICE?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: NSAIDs (e.g. naproxen), co-prescribing a PPI in the over-45s; a short-term weak opioid (codeine) if NSAIDs are insufficient/contraindicated.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which analgesic approaches does NICE advise AGAINST in low back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Do NOT routinely offer paracetamol alone, and avoid strong opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids for low back pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Why is bed rest avoided in mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: It worsens outcomes — staying active and continuing normal activities is the cornerstone of management.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the urgent treatments for the key red-flag conditions?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Cauda equina → emergency decompression; metastatic spinal cord compression → dexamethasone + MRI + oncology; discitis → antibiotics.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Leg pain from compression/irritation of a lumbosacral nerve root (radiculopathy), most often from a prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc — causing dermatomal leg pain with neurological deficits.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'core concept' of sciatica from a prolapsed disc?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: A disc's nucleus pulposus herniates (usually posterolaterally, at L4/5 or L5/S1) → compresses the adjacent nerve root → pain, sensory change, weakness and reflex loss in that root's dermatome/myotome — so the picture is radicular (dermatomal) leg pain > back pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the commonest cause of sciatica, and at which levels?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: A prolapsed (herniated) intervertebral disc, typically at L4/5 or L5/S1.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the other causes of sciatica besides a prolapsed disc?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis (vertebral slippage), tumour (especially metastasis), abscess and trauma.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the sensory, reflex and motor features of an L3 root lesion?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sensory: top of the knee; reflex: knee (L3/4); motor: knee extension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the sensory, reflex and motor features of an L4 root lesion?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sensory: medial shin/ankle; reflex: knee (L3/4); motor: knee extension and ankle dorsiflexion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the sensory, reflex and motor features of an L5 root lesion?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sensory: big toe + dorsum of foot; reflex: none; motor: big toe/foot dorsiflexion (foot drop).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the sensory, reflex and motor features of an S1 root lesion?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sensory: small toe/lateral foot; reflex: ankle (S1/2); motor: plantarflexion and foot eversion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the dermatome mnemonics for L3, L5 and S1?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: L3 = 'top of my knee'; L5 (big toe) = the largest of the 5; S1 (small toe) = the Smallest 1.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the reflex level mnemonics?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: S1/2 'buckle my shoe' (ankle); L3/4 'kick the door' (knee); C5/6 'pick up sticks' (biceps); C7/8 'lay them straight' (triceps).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which root lesion causes foot drop and loss of the ankle jerk respectively?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: L5 lesion → foot drop (weak dorsiflexion); S1 lesion → lost ankle jerk (weak plantarflexion, lateral foot sensory loss).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What features should always be screened for in sciatica (the cauda equina fork)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica, bilateral/severe leg weakness and reduced anal tone → EMERGENCY MRI + decompression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the characteristic pain pattern of sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Dermatomal leg pain radiating down the leg (leg pain usually worse than back pain), often worse on sitting, sharp/burning/shooting/electric-shock-like, radiating below the knee (true sciatica goes below the knee), ± paraesthesia/numbness/weakness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the straight leg raise (SLR) test, and when is it positive?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Passively raising the straight leg reproduces the radicular pain (stretching the nerve root) → positive in L5/S1 radiculopathy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is sciatica diagnosed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Clinically — from the radicular pattern plus neurological exam (dermatome, reflex, myotome, SLR).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: When should MRI be done in sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Not early — MRI only if symptoms persist beyond ~4–6 weeks (most resolve), or urgently if there are red flags (cauda equina symptoms → immediate MRI).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the KEY NICE point about drug management of sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Use the SAME drugs as for back pain without sciatica — first-line NSAIDs (± PPI) — NOT gabapentin/pregabalin/duloxetine (neuropathic agents are no longer recommended for sciatica).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the overall management of sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Manage like ordinary mechanical back pain — reassurance, stay active (avoid bed rest), physiotherapy and NSAIDs (± PPI); MRI/specialist referral if persistent; escalation to epidural corticosteroid injection and surgery (microdiscectomy) for refractory/severe cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the escalation pathway for persistent or refractory sciatica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Persistent/severe radicular pain → specialist referral; epidural corticosteroid injection; and surgery (microdiscectomy) for a confirmed disc prolapse with persistent/severe symptoms or a progressive deficit.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What sciatica features warrant URGENT surgery?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Progressive motor weakness or cauda equina syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Does true sciatica pain radiate above or below the knee?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Below the knee — true sciatica radiates below the knee in a nerve-root distribution.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Narrowing of the central spinal canal (by degenerative change, disc prolapse or tumour) → compressing the nerve roots/cauda equina → neurogenic claudication.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'core concept' of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: The lumbar canal is progressively narrowed (usually by age-related degeneration — thickened ligamentum flavum, facet hypertrophy, bulging discs, osteophytes) → squeezing the nerve roots, worse when the canal narrows on standing/extension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the signature clinical feature of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Neurogenic claudication — back + leg pain on walking/standing, relieved by sitting or bending forward (which opens the canal).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'shopping trolley sign'?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Leaning forward on a shopping trolley relieves the symptoms of lumbar spinal stenosis (forward flexion opens the canal).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is neurogenic claudication relieved, compared with vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Neurogenic is relieved by SITTING/bending forward (flexion opens the canal); vascular is relieved by standing still/rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'uphill paradox' distinguishing neurogenic from vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Spinal stenosis is EASIER walking uphill (forward-flexed posture opens the canal), whereas vascular claudication is worse uphill (increased muscle demand).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How do pulses and ABPI differ between neurogenic and vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Neurogenic (stenosis): normal pulses and ABPI; vascular (PAD): reduced/absent pulses and a low ABPI.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How does the offset of symptoms differ between neurogenic and vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Neurogenic is slower to ease (minutes); vascular eases quickly with rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What other features accompany neurogenic vs vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Neurogenic: back pain and neurological symptoms; vascular: trophic skin changes and a cold foot.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the commonest cause of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Degenerative (age-related) canal narrowing — facet osteoarthritis/hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum thickening, disc bulging and osteophytes.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the other causes of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Disc prolapse, tumour, spondylolisthesis, a congenitally narrow canal, and Paget's disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the clinical features of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: A combination of back pain and neuropathic leg pain/heaviness/paraesthesia on walking or standing (neurogenic claudication), symptoms better when sitting, and easier walking uphill than downhill — typically in older patients.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which investigation is the imaging of choice for lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: MRI — it demonstrates the canal narrowing (level, degree and cause).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What must be assessed to exclude the key differential of vascular claudication?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Peripheral pulses and the ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) — normal in neurogenic, reduced in vascular claudication.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the management principle for lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Conservative first (analgesia, physiotherapy, exercise); decompressive surgery (laminectomy) for refractory/severe cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What conservative measures are used for lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Analgesia, physiotherapy and flexion-based exercise, activity modification, weight loss, and (with variable evidence) epidural steroid injections.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the surgical treatment for refractory lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Decompressive laminectomy — removing lamina ± ligamentum flavum/osteophytes to widen the canal — for severe/refractory symptoms or significant neurological compromise.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What must always be screened for in severe central lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Cauda equina syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which type of exercise is preferred in lumbar spinal stenosis, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Flexion-based exercise — spinal flexion opens the narrowed canal and relieves symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the classic patient with lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: An older patient with bilateral leg pain/heaviness on walking, relieved by sitting or bending forward, and easier walking uphill.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Infection of the intervertebral disc space (often with adjacent vertebral involvement = spondylodiscitis / vertebral osteomyelitis), which can lead to sepsis or an epidural abscess.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'core concept' of discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Bacteria seed the disc space (usually haematogenously, from a distant source) → local infection → severe back pain + systemic sepsis, and it can spread into the epidural space (abscess) → cord/nerve compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the two dominant threads in managing discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: (1) It's a 'don't miss' — a septic patient with severe back pain ± new neurology needs MRI + blood cultures; and (2) because it's haematogenous, you must hunt for the ORIGIN — especially infective endocarditis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the commonest causative organism of discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Staphylococcus aureus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is discitis distinguished from mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Discitis: severe, unremitting night pain, fever/rigors/sepsis, changing lower-limb neurology, with risk factors (IVDU, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteraemia) → MRI + blood cultures. Mechanical: movement-related pain that eases with rest, no systemic features, normal neurology → reassure + analgesia.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the classic triad of discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Severe back pain + systemic sepsis (fever/rigors) + neurological symptoms (e.g. changing lower-limb neurology).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How does discitis usually reach the spine, and what does this imply?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Haematogenous seeding of the vertebrae — so the bacteria could have come from elsewhere, meaning you MUST look for the primary source (especially infective endocarditis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the risk factors for discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: IV drug use, immunosuppression, diabetes, recent bacteraemia/sepsis, spinal surgery/instrumentation, indwelling lines and endocarditis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What do new or changing lower-limb neurological symptoms in discitis suggest?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: An epidural abscess compressing the cord/roots → a surgical emergency.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which is the most sensitive investigation for discitis, and what does it show?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: MRI — it shows infection in the disc space and surrounding inflammation and identifies an epidural abscess/cord compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the role of CT-guided biopsy in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: To identify the organism and guide antimicrobial management.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Why is echocardiography (TTE/TOE) performed in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Because discitis is usually haematogenous, echocardiography assesses for infective endocarditis as the source.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What blood tests are done in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Blood cultures (before antibiotics) plus raised inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) and WCC.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the management principle for discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Identify the organism, then a prolonged course of IV antibiotics; surgery for abscess/compression; and treat the source.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Why should cultures/biopsy be obtained BEFORE antibiotics in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: So treatment is organism-directed — cultures/biopsy taken before antibiotics (where safe) identify the organism to guide therapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the typical antibiotic course for discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: A prolonged (6–8 week) IV course covering Staphylococcus aureus (e.g. flucloxacillin).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: When is surgery indicated in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: For an epidural abscess, cord compression or spinal instability (an emergency if there is a neurological deficit) — surgical drainage/decompression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is the source and sepsis addressed in discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: ABCDE / sepsis six, treat infective endocarditis or the primary source if found, plus supportive care and spinal bracing as needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the key complications of discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sepsis and an epidural abscess (→ cord compression — an emergency).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Summarise the investigation set for discitis.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: MRI (most sensitive) + blood cultures + CT-guided biopsy (organism) + echocardiography (exclude endocarditis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: A fragility fracture of a vertebral body — in osteoporosis there is an increased likelihood of fragility fractures, and the vertebrae are a very common site (the commonest osteoporotic fracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the 'core concept' of an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: The weakened vertebral body collapses under minimal load (a fragility fracture — from low-energy trauma or even normal activity like bending/coughing); it typically wedges (crushes anteriorly), giving acute back pain (though often silent) and, cumulatively, progressive height loss + kyphosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the three priorities when an osteoporotic vertebral fracture is found?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Recognise it (often incidental), exclude a sinister cause (malignancy — MRI to differentiate), and treat the underlying osteoporosis to prevent the next fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is an osteoporotic fracture distinguished from a pathological (sinister) fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Osteoporotic: low-energy/fragility trauma, no red flags, thoracolumbar junction, benign MRI marrow pattern. Pathological: red flags (age, previous cancer, night pain, systemic symptoms, neurology), any level (posterior elements suggest malignancy), tumour/infection features on MRI.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Which imaging differentiates an osteoporotic fracture from one caused by tumour?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: MRI — showing a benign marrow pattern versus tumour/infection features (also acute vs old).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What should a vertebral fracture with new neurological symptoms prompt?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Exclusion of cord/cauda equina compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What are the risk factors for an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Those of osteoporosis — advancing age (women 65+, men 75+), low BMI, previous fragility fracture, family history of hip fracture, prolonged glucocorticoid use, smoking, alcohol, falls and secondary osteoporosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: Can osteoporotic vertebral fractures be asymptomatic?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Yes — many are silent and found incidentally on imaging; height loss + kyphosis may be the only sign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the acute symptom of an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Sudden acute back pain, which may follow minimal trauma or bending.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What non-back symptoms can result from multiple osteoporotic vertebral fractures?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Breathing difficulties (from kyphosis/reduced thoracic volume) and GI issues (abdominal compression → early satiety, reflux).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What examination findings suggest an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Loss of height (vertebral compression → reduced spine length), thoracic kyphosis ('dowager's hump' from multiple thoracic wedge fractures), and localised tenderness over the spinous process at the fracture site.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is a 'dowager's hump'?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: The thoracic kyphosis produced by multiple thoracic wedge (osteoporotic) fractures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the first-line imaging for an osteoporotic vertebral fracture, and the classic finding?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: X-ray of the spine — showing WEDGING of the vertebra from compression (the classic anterior wedge fracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the role of CT and MRI in a vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: CT gives detailed bony detail/retropulsion; MRI differentiates fractures caused by other pathology (tumour) and distinguishes benign vs pathological / acute vs old.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is the underlying osteoporosis assessed after a vertebral fragility fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: DEXA + FRAX/QFracture — a fragility fracture mandates osteoporosis assessment/treatment (a fracture over age 50 lets you arrange DEXA without a risk calculation first).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What bloods screen for secondary/pathological causes of an atypical vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Calcium/phosphate/ALP/PTH, a myeloma screen, PSA and vitamin D.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the management principle for an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Analgesia + early mobilisation for the acute fracture, AND treat the underlying osteoporosis to prevent the next; vertebroplasty/surgery in selected cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: How is the acute fracture managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Adequate analgesia + early mobilisation (avoid prolonged bed rest → deconditioning/bone loss) + physiotherapy; most stable fractures heal conservatively over weeks.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: What is the KEY step to prevent recurrence after an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Treat the osteoporosis — calcium + vitamin D + a bisphosphonate, and address risk factors (a fragility fracture is a strong indication for treatment).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.front: When are vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty and surgery indicated?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.back: Vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty (cement injection) for severe, persistent pain not responding to conservative treatment; surgery for instability, neurological compromise (cord/cauda compression) or a pathological fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: A common overuse/friction injury causing LATERAL knee pain, especially in runners.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What is the 'core concept' of ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: The iliotibial band (ITB) runs down the outside of the thigh (from tensor fasciae latae/gluteus maximus to Gerdy's tubercle just below the lateral knee); repeated knee flexion/extension makes it rub against the lateral femoral epicondyle → friction, irritation and pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: Where does the iliotibial band run and insert?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: From tensor fasciae latae and gluteus maximus down the lateral thigh to Gerdy's tubercle, just below the lateral knee.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What is the classic exam equation for ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Long-distance runner + lateral knee pain = ITB syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: Where is the characteristic point of tenderness in ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: 2–3 cm ABOVE the lateral joint line, over the lateral femoral epicondyle.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What are the risk factors for ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Overuse/training errors (long-distance running, sudden mileage increases, cycling, downhill running) and biomechanical factors (weak hip abductors/gluteus medius, genu varum, excessive foot pronation, cambered surfaces, a tight ITB).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: Which muscle weakness is a key biomechanical risk factor for ITBS?
What is the character and pattern of the pain in ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Sharp/burning lateral knee pain, worse with running (especially at ~30° of knee flexion), worse downhill or on stairs; it comes on after a predictable distance and eases with rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: At roughly what knee flexion angle is ITBS pain worst?
Why is the absence of an effusion and of locking/catching important in ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: It distinguishes ITBS from intra-articular pathology (e.g. a meniscal tear).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: How is ITBS distinguished from a lateral meniscal tear?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: ITBS gives tenderness 2–3 cm ABOVE the joint line from overuse, whereas a meniscal tear gives lateral joint-LINE pain with locking/catching after a twisting injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: How is ITBS distinguished from patellofemoral pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Patellofemoral pain is anterior/around the patella, whereas ITBS is lateral with tenderness above the joint line.
Clinically — the runner history plus characteristic lateral tenderness (± Noble's test); imaging is not routinely needed.
Pressure over the lateral femoral epicondyle while extending the flexed knee reproduces the pain — supporting ITBS.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: When is imaging used in ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Only if the diagnosis is unclear or to exclude other pathology (e.g. a meniscal tear) in refractory cases — MRI or ultrasound.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What is the overall management principle for ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Conservative — activity modification + stretching + hip-abductor strengthening; most resolve conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What activity modifications are advised in ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Relative rest, cut mileage, avoid downhill running, then a graded return; analgesia/NSAIDs and ice after activity.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What is the KEY active treatment for ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Physiotherapy — ITB and hip stretching AND hip-abductor (gluteus medius) strengthening, plus gait/technique and biomechanical correction, and foam rolling.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.front: What are the options for refractory ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.back: Occasional corticosteroid injection to the point of friction; surgery (ITB release/lengthening) is a rare last resort.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What kinds of conditions are covered by 'hand & wrist disorders'?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Common non-traumatic hand and wrist soft-tissue conditions affecting the tendon sheaths, palmar fascia and joint/tendon cysts.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the organising principle for hand & wrist disorders?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: They are largely clinical diagnoses; most respond to conservative measures or steroid injection, with surgery reserved for refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the pathology and clue for De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Inflammation of the first extensor compartment (APL/EPB) sheath → radial wrist pain, a positive Finkelstein's test; classically new mothers.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the pathology and clue for Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Palmar fascia fibrosis → fixed flexion of the ring/little finger; associated with alcohol, diabetes and family history.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the pathology and clue for trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A flexor tendon nodule at the A1 pulley → the finger clicks/locks in flexion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the pathology and clue for a ganglion cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A mucin-filled cyst arising from a joint or tendon sheath → a firm swelling that transilluminates, often on the dorsal wrist.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the general first-line management across hand & wrist disorders?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Reassurance plus a splint or steroid injection for most; ganglia frequently resolve spontaneously.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Swelling and inflammation of the tendon sheaths of abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) at the wrist — a repetitive strain injury causing pain on the RADIAL side of the wrist.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Which two tendons are involved in De Quervain's, and where do they run?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB), which run together through the first dorsal (extensor) compartment at the radial wrist, beneath the extensor retinaculum.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the 'core concept' of De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Repetitive thumb/wrist movement inflames and swells the shared APL/EPB sheath → the tendons no longer glide smoothly through the tight first compartment → radial-sided wrist pain worse with thumb/wrist movement (a stenosing tenosynovitis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Who classically develops De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: People with repetitive thumb use — new mothers (lifting babies), texting/typing and occupational tasks ('mother's thumb' / 'gamer's thumb').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What are the clinical features of De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Radial wrist pain near the base of the thumb (may radiate up the forearm; aching/burning), tenderness over the radial styloid (the characteristic tender spot ± local swelling), and painful thumb abduction against resistance (worse with gripping/lifting/wringing).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Where is the characteristic tender spot in De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Over the radial styloid.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is Finkelstein's test, and what is a positive result?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The patient makes a fist with the thumb tucked INSIDE the fingers, then the wrist is adducted (ulnar deviated), straining the APL + EPB tendons; a positive result is pain at the radial wrist — confirming De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: How is De Quervain's diagnosed, and when is imaging used?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: It is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by Finkelstein's test; imaging is not routinely needed — ultrasound only if unclear (shows tendon sheath thickening/fluid).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: How is De Quervain's distinguished from thumb-base (CMC) osteoarthritis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: CMC osteoarthritis gives pain and squaring at the CMC joint in older patients with a positive grind test, whereas De Quervain's gives radial styloid tenderness with a positive Finkelstein's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: How is De Quervain's distinguished from a scaphoid fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A scaphoid fracture has anatomical snuffbox tenderness and a FOOSH history, whereas De Quervain's has radial styloid tenderness and pain on thumb movement with positive Finkelstein's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is intersection syndrome, as a differential for De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Pain more proximal/dorsal in the forearm from the second-compartment crossover (where the first and second compartments intersect).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is Wartenberg's syndrome, as a differential for radial wrist symptoms?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Radial sensory neuritis — numbness/tingling with a positive Tinel's sign (rather than the movement-related pain of De Quervain's).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the management of De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Conservative — rest/activity modification, a thumb spica splint (± physiotherapy) and analgesia/NSAIDs → corticosteroid injection into the first extensor compartment (often highly effective) → surgical release of the extensor retinaculum if refractory.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What splint is used in De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A thumb spica splint (immobilises the thumb and wrist).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Why do pregnancy/lactation-related cases of De Quervain's often improve without surgery?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: They often resolve once the precipitant (e.g. baby-lifting during lactation) settles.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A progressive fibrosis (fibromatosis) of the palmar fascia — the fascia becomes thickened and tight, forming nodules and cords that pull the fingers into flexion (a contracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the 'core concept' of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The palmar fascia thickens, develops nodules and forms cords that extend into the fingers and pull them into flexion — so the finger cannot fully extend.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the typical clinical picture of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A painless, slowly progressive flexion contracture, usually of the ring finger, in a patient with typical risk factors (family history, alcohol, diabetes).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Which finger is most commonly affected in Dupuytren's, and which is least?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The ring finger (± little finger) is most commonly affected; the index finger is least likely to be affected.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Is Dupuytren's contracture usually painful?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: No — it is usually painLESS; it is loss of extension, not pain, that brings patients in (a key discriminator from tenosynovitis/trigger finger).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the first sign of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Hard nodules on the palm.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What skin changes occur in Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Skin thickening and pitting (puckering) over the palm.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Describe the progression of Dupuytren's contracture.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Hard palmar nodules → the fascia slowly thickens and forms cords → the finger is pulled into flexion → eventually it becomes impossible to fully extend the finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What are the causes/risk factors for Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A positive family history (autosomal dominant, strongly hereditary), phenytoin (the classic drug cause), manual labour (especially with vibrating tools), alcoholic liver disease/alcohol excess, diabetes mellitus and hand trauma.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Which drug is the classic cause of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Phenytoin.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the classic patient with Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: An older man of Northern European descent, often with alcohol excess or diabetes.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the inheritance pattern of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Autosomal dominant (strongly hereditary).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: How is Dupuytren's contracture diagnosed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Clinically — a palpable cord/nodule plus the table-top test; no imaging or bloods are needed (consider screening for associated conditions such as diabetes and alcohol/liver disease).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the table-top test, and what is a positive result?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The patient tries to place the hands FLAT on a table; a positive result is being unable to rest the hand completely flat — indicating a significant contracture and a marker for surgical referral.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the functional threshold that triggers surgical treatment in Dupuytren's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: When the MCP joints cannot be straightened and the hand cannot be placed flat on a table (a positive table-top test).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the management of MILD Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Observe/monitor; hand therapy and stretching; collagenase injection (enzymatic cord dissolution) is a non-surgical alternative in some settings.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What are the three surgical procedures for Dupuytren's, in increasing invasiveness?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Needle fasciotomy (aponeurotomy) — a needle divides/loosens the cord (least invasive); limited fasciectomy — removing the abnormal fascia and cord; dermofasciectomy — removing the fascia, cord AND overlying skin with a skin graft (most extensive, for recurrent/severe disease).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is a needle fasciotomy (aponeurotomy)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The least invasive surgical option — a needle is used to divide and loosen the Dupuytren's cord.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is a dermofasciectomy, and when is it used?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The most extensive procedure — removing the fascia, cord AND the overlying skin with a skin graft — used for recurrent/severe Dupuytren's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Does Dupuytren's contracture recur after treatment?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Yes — Dupuytren's tends to recur after treatment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the key discriminator between Dupuytren's contracture and trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with no catching/snapping, whereas trigger finger causes painful catching/clicking/locking.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Pain and difficulty moving a finger from a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the pulleys it passes through — the tendon becomes stuck and can't pass smoothly through the pulley.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the 'core concept' of trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The flexor tendons run through pulleys holding them against bone; if the tendon (or sheath) thickens — often forming a nodule — it no longer glides through the tight first (A1) pulley at the MCP joint → the finger catches, locks in flexion, then releases suddenly with a painful pop/click.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the signature presentation of trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A finger that catches/locks in a bent position and snaps straight, worst in the morning.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Which pulley is most commonly involved in trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The first annular (A1) pulley at the MCP joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Explain the mechanism of the 'trigger' in trigger finger.
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: When the finger is flexed, the tendon nodule sits proximal to the A1 pulley; as the finger extends, the nodule gets stuck at the entrance to the A1 pulley → the finger locks in flexion, then releases suddenly with a painful pop/click.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Which digits are most commonly affected in trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: The thumb, middle or ring finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Where is the pain/tenderness in trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Around the MCP joint on the PALM side, where a nodule may be felt at the base of the affected finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: When are trigger finger symptoms typically worst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: In the morning, improving during the day.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What are the risk factors for trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Idiopathic in most; associations include female sex, rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes mellitus (the 'diabetic hand').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: How is trigger finger diagnosed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: Clinically — the trigger (catching/locking that releases with a snap) plus a palpable nodule; no imaging is needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the first-line treatment for trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath at the A1 pulley — successful in most patients.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What role does a splint play in trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A finger splint may be applied (holding the finger in extension, especially at night), along with activity modification and NSAIDs.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: What is the surgical treatment for refractory trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.back: A1 pulley release — dividing the A1 pulley to free the tendon — used only if steroid injection fails.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.front: Summarise the management ladder for trigger finger.
