conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: Why is meralgia paraesthetica worse on standing and better on sitting?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Standing/hip extension stretches the nerve (worsening symptoms), whereas sitting/hip flexion relaxes it (relieving symptoms).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: How is meralgia paraesthetica distinguished from an L2/L3 radiculopathy or femoral neuropathy?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Those have MOTOR weakness (hip flexion/knee extension weakness, reflex changes, back pain); meralgia is purely sensory with a well-demarcated cutaneous distribution and NO motor weakness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: What examination finding reproduces the symptoms of meralgia paraesthetica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Deep palpation just below the ASIS plus hip extension reproduces the lateral-thigh symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: What is the pelvic compression test?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: A very sensitive test that compresses the pelvis to relax the inguinal ligament and relieve the symptoms — often diagnostic on its own.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: How is meralgia paraesthetica confirmed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Largely clinically; a diagnostic local anaesthetic nerve block abolishes the pain (confirmatory and can be therapeutic); ultrasound aids diagnosis and guides injection; NCS/imaging only if atypical (to exclude an L2/3 lesion).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: What is the first-line management of meralgia paraesthetica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Conservative — remove the compressive cause: weight loss, loose clothing (avoid tight belts), activity modification, reassurance (usually benign and self-limiting; pregnancy-related resolves after delivery), and analgesia ± neuropathic agents (amitriptyline, gabapentin/pregabalin).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: What is the second-line treatment for meralgia paraesthetica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: A local anaesthetic ± corticosteroid injection (nerve block — diagnostic and therapeutic, can be ultrasound-guided).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: When is surgery considered in meralgia paraesthetica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Rarely — for severe, persistent, refractory cases: nerve decompression or (rarely) transection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.front: What is the escalation ladder for meralgia paraesthetica?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Compression Ne.back: Conservative (weight loss, loose clothing, analgesia) → nerve block → surgery if refractory.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is a Charcot joint (neuropathic arthropathy)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: A progressive degeneration of a weight-bearing joint secondary to a LOSS OF SENSATION — the joint becomes badly disrupted and destroyed because the underlying neuropathy removes its protection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the 'core concept' of a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: You protect your joints because they hurt — lose the protective pain and proprioceptive sensation and the joint suffers repeated unnoticed micro-trauma → it progressively breaks down, fragments and dislocates, all while the patient feels relatively little pain (the paradox).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the single most useful clue to a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: The mismatch — a grossly swollen, warm, deformed, destroyed joint that hurts far LESS than it should.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the commonest modern setting for a Charcot joint?
What is the key clinical challenge with a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Distinguishing it from infection (osteomyelitis/cellulitis), which it closely mimics — both give a hot, swollen foot — but management is opposite.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: How is a Charcot foot distinguished from infection?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Charcot = relatively PAINLESS (out of proportion to destruction), usually systemically well (no fever), intact skin (no wound), redness/swelling often SETTLES on elevation, and usually normal/mildly raised inflammatory markers; infection = more painful, fever, a skin break/ulcer, does not settle on elevation, raised WCC/CRP (the two can coexist).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the high-yield rule distinguishing Charcot from infection?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: A hot, swollen, red foot that is relatively PAINLESS with intact skin, settling on elevation, in a diabetic = Charcot foot; fever + a skin break/ulcer + raised inflammatory markers point to infection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What are the causes of a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Any condition causing a peripheral (sensory) neuropathy — diabetic neuropathy (commonest), alcoholic neuropathy, syphilis (tabes dorsalis, the classic historical cause), leprosy, spinal cord injury/syringomyelia, B12 deficiency (SACD), Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and spina bifida.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: Which conditions classically cause UPPER-LIMB Charcot joints?
What is the paradoxical presentation of a Charcot foot?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: A hot, swollen, red, warm foot with disproportionately little pain — the pain is mild for the degree of destruction (the key clue).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What deformity develops as a Charcot foot progresses?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Gross deformity — the midfoot collapses → a 'rocker-bottom foot' (loss of the arch), with joint instability and ulceration over the deformity (→ infection risk).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What does X-ray show in a Charcot joint (the '6 Ds')?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Osteolysis, joint dislocation and extensive bone remodelling/fragmentation — Destruction, Dislocation, Debris, Disorganisation, increased Density (sclerosis) and Distension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the role of MRI in a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: For early disease (before X-ray changes) and to help distinguish Charcot from osteomyelitis (a key clinical difficulty).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What investigations assess the underlying neuropathy in a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Monofilament/vibration testing (to confirm sensory loss) and glucose/HbA1c; also exclude infection (WCC/CRP, look for a wound/ulcer).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the overarching management principle for a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: OFFLOAD the joint (immobilise/non-weight-bear) + treat the underlying neuropathy + protect the skin — a 'don't miss, offload early' diagnosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What is the key intervention in a Charcot joint, and why is it time-critical?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Offloading — immobilisation + non-weight-bearing with a total contact cast (or removable walker) during the acute (hot, active) phase; early offloading preserves joint architecture, whereas delay leads to progressive collapse and deformity.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: What broader measures are used in managing a Charcot foot?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: Optimise glycaemic control and manage the neuropathy (treat B12 deficiency/syphilis if relevant); a diabetic foot MDT (podiatry, diabetology, orthotics), custom footwear/orthotics, and regular foot care/ulcer prevention (high ulcer/amputation risk); bisphosphonates are sometimes used (limited evidence).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.front: When is surgery indicated in a Charcot joint?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Charcot Joint.back: For severe deformity, instability or non-healing ulceration (reconstruction/arthrodesis; occasionally amputation), and to treat coexisting infection if present.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: A popliteal cyst — a fluid-filled swelling behind the knee; not a true cyst but a distension of the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the 'core concept' of a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Synovial fluid from the knee joint accumulates in (or communicates with) the gastrocnemius–semimembranosus bursa in the popliteal fossa — essentially fluid bulging out at the back of the knee.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What are the two clinical priorities with a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: (1) Distinguish primary (benign, children) from secondary (a marker of underlying joint pathology, adults); and (2) recognise that a RUPTURED cyst mimics a DVT.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is a PRIMARY Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: One with no underlying pathology, usually in children — benign and needs no treatment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is a SECONDARY Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: One due to an underlying condition (e.g. osteoarthritis), usually in adults — a marker of intra-articular knee pathology.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What conditions are associated with a secondary Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, meniscal tears and gout.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What does a Baker's cyst signal in an adult?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Knee joint pathology — look for osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis or a meniscal tear.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What are the clinical features of a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: A swelling in the popliteal fossa (behind the knee), often fluctuant, more prominent on standing/knee extension and softening or disappearing on flexion (Foucher's sign); it may be asymptomatic or cause posterior knee discomfort/tightness, a mass sensation, or restricted flexion.
The Baker's cyst is more prominent on knee extension and softens/disappears on flexion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the most important complication of a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Rupture — it produces symptoms similar to a DVT (acute calf pain, redness and swelling), making it a key DVT differential.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: How do you distinguish a ruptured Baker's cyst from a DVT?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: They are clinically indistinguishable — both cause acute calf pain/swelling/redness; a ruptured cyst is a diagnosis made AFTER excluding DVT (Wells score, D-dimer, Doppler ultrasound).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the high-yield rule about a ruptured Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: It mimics a DVT → always consider and EXCLUDE a DVT in acute calf swelling; you cannot assume it is a burst cyst (though most ruptures are actually asymptomatic).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the first-line investigation for a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Ultrasound — confirms the cyst (fluid-filled), assesses for rupture, and helps exclude a DVT (no clot).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: When is MRI used for a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: If there is diagnostic doubt, or to assess the underlying knee pathology (meniscal tear, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis) in secondary cysts.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the management principle for a Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: No treatment needed in children; treat the underlying cause in adults; exclude DVT if ruptured.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: How is a symptomatic or large Baker's cyst managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Analgesia and activity modification; ultrasound-guided aspiration ± corticosteroid injection for a large/symptomatic cyst; occasionally surgical excision (recurrent/refractory, with intra-articular pathology addressed).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.front: What is the key to managing and preventing recurrence of a secondary Baker's cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Baker's Cyst.back: Treating the underlying knee pathology (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, meniscal tear or gout).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is avascular necrosis (AVN)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Also called osteonecrosis — death of bone tissue secondary to loss of its blood supply → bone destruction and loss of joint function.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the 'core concept' of AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Bone is living tissue that depends on a blood supply — interrupt it (steroids, alcohol, trauma…) and the bone infarcts, dies and collapses, destroying the overlying joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the classic and commonest site of AVN, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: The femoral head (hip) — its blood supply is precarious, largely retrograde via the medial circumflex femoral artery, and easily disrupted.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What are the clinical priorities in AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: It is initially silent and X-ray-negative, so: think of it in the at-risk patient (steroids, alcohol, a fractured hip) with new joint pain, image early with MRI (detects it before X-ray changes), and intervene before the joint collapses.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: Besides the hip, what other sites are prone to AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: The femoral condyles (knee), humeral head, scaphoid and talus — all with a tenuous blood supply.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What are the two commonest ATRAUMATIC causes of AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Long-term steroid use (the commonest atraumatic cause) and alcohol excess.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the commonest TRAUMATIC cause of AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: A displaced femoral neck fracture / hip dislocation, which disrupts the femoral head's blood supply.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What does the 'ASEPTIC' mnemonic list as causes of AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Alcohol/APS and SLE, Sickle cell disease (vaso-occlusion)/Steroids, the bEnds (decompression sickness/caisson disease), Pancreatitis, Trauma/radiation, Idiopathic, Caisson/Gaucher's disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: Why is a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture treated with replacement rather than fixation in older patients?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Because it carries a high AVN risk (disrupted femoral head blood supply) → hemiarthroplasty/THR is preferred over fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What are the clinical features of AVN over time?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Initially asymptomatic (the pre-collapse phase is silent), then pain in the joint (for the hip, groin/hip pain worse on weight-bearing and movement, progressive), and later reduced range of movement, limp and stiffness as the bone collapses with secondary osteoarthritis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the high-yield clinical rule for AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: An at-risk patient (steroids/alcohol/prior hip fracture) with new, progressive, insidious hip or groin pain = AVN until proven otherwise — image early, before X-ray changes.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What does a plain X-ray show in AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: It may be NORMAL initially (early AVN is X-ray-negative); later sclerosis and an irregular articular surface, subchondral fracture and flattening, with the affected head appearing smaller than the other side.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the 'crescent sign' in AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: A subchondral lucency on X-ray indicating subchondral collapse — a classic sign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the gold-standard investigation for AVN, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: MRI — the most sensitive test; it detects AVN early, before X-ray changes appear, allowing joint-preserving intervention.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: How is AVN staged, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: On X-ray/MRI findings (e.g. the Ficat classification) — this guides whether to attempt joint preservation or proceed to replacement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the high-yield imaging rule for AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: X-ray may be normal early → if AVN is suspected, get an MRI (gold standard, detects it early).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the overarching management principle for AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Early/pre-collapse → joint-preserving measures; late/collapsed joint → joint replacement; and always address the underlying cause.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: How is EARLY (pre-collapse) AVN managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Address the cause (reduce/stop steroids, reduce alcohol), protected weight-bearing + analgesia, and core decompression — drilling the necrotic segment to relieve pressure and promote revascularisation (± bone grafting); bisphosphonates may slow progression (limited evidence).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is core decompression?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Drilling the necrotic bone segment to relieve pressure and promote revascularisation (± bone grafting) — a joint-preserving procedure for early disease before collapse.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: How is LATE (collapsed/advanced) AVN managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Joint replacement — total hip replacement (THR) is the definitive treatment for a collapsed femoral head / secondary osteoarthritis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the staging principle that guides AVN management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Pre-collapse → joint-preserving (core decompression); post-collapse → joint replacement — hence the value of early MRI diagnosis to catch it before collapse.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: Which artery provides the main (precarious) blood supply to the femoral head?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: The medial circumflex femoral artery — supplying the femoral head largely in a retrograde direction, which is why the supply is easily disrupted.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: Why does a displaced intracapsular femoral neck fracture carry a high AVN risk, but an extracapsular fracture does not?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: The retrograde blood supply to the femoral head runs within the capsule, so an intracapsular displaced fracture disrupts it; extracapsular fractures spare this supply, so they are fixed rather than replaced.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is 'dysbaric' osteonecrosis (the bends)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: AVN caused by nitrogen bubbles obstructing bone blood vessels in decompression sickness (caisson disease) — a recognised cause of osteonecrosis in divers.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: Why does Gaucher's disease cause AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Accumulation of lipid-laden Gaucher cells in the marrow raises intraosseous pressure and compromises the bone's blood supply, causing osteonecrosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.front: What is the significance of bilateral AVN?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Avascular Necr.back: Atraumatic causes (steroids, alcohol, sickle cell, SLE, Gaucher's) often affect both hips → bilateral AVN suggests a systemic/atraumatic cause and warrants imaging the other hip.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A 68-year-old woman falls onto an outstretched hand and has a painful, swollen wrist with an upturned 'dinner fork' deformity. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Colles' fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A FOOSH with dorsal displacement giving a dinner-fork deformity, in an older osteoporotic woman, is a Colles' fracture (the commonest distal radius fracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: In which direction is the distal fragment displaced in a Colles' fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Dorsal (posterior)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A Colles' fracture has dorsal (posterior) displacement + angulation, producing the dinner-fork deformity.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A patient falls onto a flexed wrist and X-ray shows volar angulation of a distal radius fracture. What is this called?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Smith's fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Volar angulation of an extra-articular distal radius fracture from a flexed-wrist injury is a Smith's fracture (reverse Colles').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which mnemonic correctly describes a Colles' fracture?
options: Dorsally Displaced Distal radius → Dinner fork Deformity
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Dorsally Displaced Distal radius → Dinner fork Deformity
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The Colles' mnemonic is 'Dorsally Displaced Distal radius → Dinner fork Deformity' (all the D's).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which nerve is most at risk in a distal radius (Colles') fracture, and what syndrome can result?
options: Median nerve — acute carpal tunnel syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Median nerve — acute carpal tunnel syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The median nerve is at risk from the fracture/swelling, causing acute carpal tunnel syndrome — assess it before and after reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why are Smith's fractures more likely than Colles' fractures to need surgical fixation?
options: They are more unstable (the volar tilt tends to displace)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: They are more unstable (the volar tilt tends to displace)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Smith's fractures are more unstable because the volar tilt tends to displace, so they more often require fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which X-ray view best distinguishes a Colles' from a Smith's fracture?
options: Lateral view (shows dorsal vs volar displacement)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Lateral view (shows dorsal vs volar displacement)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The lateral view shows the direction of displacement — dorsal (Colles') versus volar (Smith's).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A patient develops delayed loss of thumb extension weeks after a Colles' fracture. Which complication is this?
options: Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The EPL tendon can fray over the fracture callus (often delayed), causing loss of thumb extension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the initial management of a displaced Colles' fracture?
options: Closed reduction (± Bier's block) and cast, with a post-reduction X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Closed reduction (± Bier's block) and cast, with a post-reduction X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A displaced Colles' fracture is managed with closed reduction (± regional anaesthesia/Bier's block) and a cast, checking a post-reduction X-ray.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which patient/mechanism is classic for a Colles' fracture?
options: A young man falling on a flexed wrist
An osteoporotic post-menopausal woman after a FOOSH
A child with a compression injury
A footballer with a twisting knee
An elderly man with hip pain
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An osteoporotic post-menopausal woman after a FOOSH
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A Colles' fracture is classically a fragility fracture in an osteoporotic post-menopausal woman after a fall onto an outstretched hand.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A distal radius fracture is unstable and intra-articular after failed reduction. What is the appropriate management?
options: Surgery — ORIF (volar plate) or K-wires/external fixation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Surgery — ORIF (volar plate) or K-wires/external fixation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Unstable, intra-articular or failed-reduction distal radius fractures need surgery (ORIF with a volar plate, or K-wires/external fixation); Smith's often needs fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which late complication of a distal radius fracture presents with disproportionate pain, swelling and skin/temperature changes?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: CRPS is a late complication with disproportionate pain, swelling and skin/temperature changes.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: At what location do Colles' and Smith's fractures occur?
options: At the mid-shaft of the radius
About 1 inch (2.5 cm) proximal to the radiocarpal joint (extra-articular)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: About 1 inch (2.5 cm) proximal to the radiocarpal joint (extra-articular)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Both are extra-articular fractures about 1 inch (2.5 cm) proximal to the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A distal radius fracture is minimally displaced with a normal neurovascular exam. What is the appropriate management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Below-elbow cast immobilisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Undisplaced/minimally displaced distal radius fractures are managed with below-elbow cast immobilisation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Besides fracture care, what must be addressed after a fragility Colles' fracture?
options: Assess the median nerve, and treat the osteoporosis with a falls assessment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Assess the median nerve, and treat the osteoporosis with a falls assessment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A fragility Colles' fracture warrants median nerve assessment and osteoporosis treatment plus a falls assessment to prevent further fractures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What deformity is associated with a Smith's fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Garden spade (reverse Colles') deformity
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A Smith's fracture (volar angulation) produces a 'garden spade' or reverse Colles' deformity, opposite to the dinner-fork of a Colles' fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: When should repeat imaging be arranged for a suspected but radiographically inconclusive distal radius fracture?
options: In 7–10 days, after immobilising and referring
Only if pain worsens after a year
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: In 7–10 days, after immobilising and referring
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: If the initial X-ray is inconclusive, immobilise and refer, with repeat imaging in 7–10 days.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which acute complication requires assessment for possible urgent decompression after a Colles' fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Acute carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve compression from the fracture/swelling) may require urgent decompression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A 25-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and has radial-sided wrist pain. Examination shows tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, but the X-ray is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Prescribe a wrist brace and no follow-up
Order a bone scan in 6 months
Immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray at 7–10 days or MRI) — treat as a scaphoid fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Immobilise and re-image (repeat X-ray at 7–10 days or MRI) — treat as a scaphoid fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: FOOSH + snuffbox tenderness is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise; up to ~20% are X-ray-occult, so immobilise and re-image (or MRI) even with a normal initial film.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the single most important anatomical fact about the scaphoid?
options: It has a rich anterograde blood supply
It has a retrograde blood supply entering distally, so a fracture risks proximal AVN and non-union
It is supplied only from the medullary cavity
It is supplied by the ulnar artery proximally
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: It has a retrograde blood supply entering distally, so a fracture risks proximal AVN and non-union
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The scaphoid's retrograde blood supply (entering distally, flowing proximally) means a fracture starves the proximal fragment → AVN and non-union.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is the KEY clinical sign of a scaphoid fracture?
options: A palpable gap in the tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Anatomical snuffbox tenderness is the key sign of a scaphoid fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which fracture location carries the highest risk of avascular necrosis in the scaphoid?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The proximal pole
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The more proximal the fracture, the higher the AVN/non-union risk, because the retrograde blood supply enters distally.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is the definitive (most sensitive) investigation for a suspected occult scaphoid fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: MRI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: MRI is the most sensitive and definitive investigation, detecting occult fractures not seen on X-ray and assessing for AVN.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the classic mechanism of a scaphoid fracture?
options: A direct blow to the ulnar wrist
A twisting injury of the forearm
A crush injury of the fingers
A fall onto a flexed wrist
A FOOSH with the wrist hyperextended and radially deviated
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: A FOOSH with the wrist hyperextended and radially deviated
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A scaphoid fracture typically results from a FOOSH with axial compression, the wrist hyperextended and radially deviated.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the untreated end-stage complication of a scaphoid non-union?
options: SNAC wrist (scaphoid non-union advanced collapse — arthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: SNAC wrist (scaphoid non-union advanced collapse — arthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: An untreated scaphoid non-union/AVN leads to SNAC wrist — scaphoid non-union advanced collapse with wrist arthritis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: How is an undisplaced scaphoid fracture typically managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Below-elbow cast immobilisation (often 6–12 weeks)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Undisplaced scaphoid fractures are managed with below-elbow cast immobilisation, often 6–12 weeks, as they are slow to heal.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: When is surgical fixation (compression screw ± bone graft) indicated for a scaphoid fracture?
options: For displaced, proximal-pole or non-union fractures (high AVN risk)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: For displaced, proximal-pole or non-union fractures (high AVN risk)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Displaced, proximal-pole or non-union scaphoid fractures — the high-AVN-risk ones — are treated with surgical fixation (compression screw ± bone grafting).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which structure supplies the scaphoid's retrograde blood supply?
options: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery (entering distally)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery (entering distally)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The dorsal carpal branch of the radial artery enters the scaphoid distally and supplies it in a retrograde (distal-to-proximal) fashion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which examination manoeuvre, besides snuffbox tenderness, supports a scaphoid fracture?
options: Pain on axial compression (telescoping) of the thumb
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Pain on axial compression (telescoping) of the thumb
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Pain on axial compression (telescoping) of the thumb, along with snuffbox and scaphoid tubercle tenderness, supports a scaphoid fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why might a wrist joint effusion be absent in a scaphoid fracture?
options: Hyperacute (<4 h) and delayed (>4 days) presentations may not show an effusion
Effusion only occurs with a normal X-ray
It is masked by snuffbox tenderness
Effusions only occur in distal radius fractures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Hyperacute (<4 h) and delayed (>4 days) presentations may not show an effusion
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A wrist effusion may be absent in very early (<4 h) or delayed (>4 days) presentations, so its absence does not exclude a scaphoid fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is the commonest carpal bone to fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The scaphoid
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The scaphoid is the commonest carpal bone to fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A patient with snuffbox tenderness is discharged on a single normal X-ray and later develops non-union. What was the error?
options: Snuffbox tenderness should never be discharged on a single normal X-ray; it should be immobilised and re-imaged
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Snuffbox tenderness should never be discharged on a single normal X-ray; it should be immobilised and re-imaged
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH must be treated as a scaphoid fracture and immobilised with re-imaging/MRI — never discharged on a single normal X-ray.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the goal of prompt, defensive management of a suspected scaphoid fracture?
options: To prevent avascular necrosis and non-union (and subsequent arthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: To prevent avascular necrosis and non-union (and subsequent arthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The goal is to prevent AVN, non-union and later SNAC-wrist arthritis by immobilising and confirming/excluding the fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A patient falls with a rotational force and X-ray shows a distal radial shaft fracture with a prominent ulnar head at the wrist. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Galeazzi fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A radial shaft fracture with a dislocated distal radioulnar joint (prominent ulnar head) is a Galeazzi fracture ('GRUsome').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A Monteggia fracture consists of:
options: A radial shaft fracture + DRUJ dislocation
An ulnar fracture + radial head (proximal radioulnar joint) dislocation
A distal radius fracture + median nerve injury
A clavicle fracture + AC joint dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An ulnar fracture + radial head (proximal radioulnar joint) dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A Monteggia fracture is an ulnar fracture with a radial head dislocation ('MURder').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which mnemonic correctly describes a Galeazzi fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: GRUsome — Radial fracture + Ulnar-radio (DRUJ) dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: 'GRUsome' = Galeazzi: Radial fracture + Ulnar-radio (DRUJ) dislocation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which joint dislocates in a Monteggia fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The proximal radioulnar joint (radial head)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: In a Monteggia fracture the proximal radioulnar joint dislocates (the radial head), accompanying the ulnar fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which line is checked on X-ray to detect the radial head dislocation of a Monteggia fracture?
options: The radiocapitellar line (should point to the capitellum)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The radiocapitellar line (should point to the capitellum)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The radiocapitellar line through the radial head should point to the capitellum; if it does not, the radial head is dislocated (Monteggia).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why must both the elbow and the wrist be X-rayed with any single-bone forearm fracture?
options: To exclude a scaphoid fracture only
To catch the associated radioulnar joint dislocation, which is easily missed and causes disability
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: To catch the associated radioulnar joint dislocation, which is easily missed and causes disability
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A single forearm-bone fracture is often part of a fracture-dislocation, so both joints must be imaged to avoid missing the dislocation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the mechanism of a Monteggia fracture?
options: A rotational fall on the hand
A direct blow to the wrist
A fall onto a flexed wrist
An axial load with the wrist extended
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: A FOOSH with forced pronation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A Monteggia fracture typically results from a FOOSH with forced pronation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the management of a Galeazzi fracture in an adult?
options: ORIF of the radius, ensuring the DRUJ is reduced and stable
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: ORIF of the radius, ensuring the DRUJ is reduced and stable
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: In adults a Galeazzi fracture is managed with ORIF of the radius, ensuring the distal radioulnar joint is reduced and stable.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: How is a Monteggia fracture managed in an adult?
options: ORIF of the ulna (which usually relocates the radial head)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: ORIF of the ulna (which usually relocates the radial head)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: ORIF of the ulna is performed in adults; reducing the ulna usually relocates the dislocated radial head.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which nerve is particularly at risk in a Monteggia fracture, and how is it tested?
options: The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) — finger/thumb extension
The anterior interosseous nerve — pinch grip
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) — finger/thumb extension
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve is at risk from the radial head dislocation in a Monteggia fracture — test finger and thumb extension.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why are forearm fracture-dislocations often managed with closed reduction in children but ORIF in adults?
options: Children's fractures remodel and the reduction holds better
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Children's fractures remodel and the reduction holds better
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Children's fractures remodel and hold reduction well, so closed reduction is often used, whereas adults usually need ORIF.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the consequence of a missed radial head dislocation in a Monteggia fracture?
options: Chronic dislocation, deformity and impaired forearm rotation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Chronic dislocation, deformity and impaired forearm rotation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A missed radial head dislocation leads to chronic dislocation, deformity and impaired forearm rotation, so prompt diagnosis is essential.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which bone is fractured in a Galeazzi fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The radius (shaft)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The radial shaft is fractured in a Galeazzi fracture, with an associated DRUJ dislocation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A prominent ulnar head at the wrist with a distal radial fracture indicates which injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Galeazzi fracture (DRUJ dislocation)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A prominent ulnar head (DRUJ dislocation) with a distal radial shaft fracture is a Galeazzi fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the core anatomical principle explaining why one forearm-bone fracture is often accompanied by a joint dislocation?
options: The forearm has only one bone
The radius and ulna form a ring joined at both ends, so breaking one bone tends to dislocate a joint at the other end
The bones share one joint only
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The radius and ulna form a ring joined at both ends, so breaking one bone tends to dislocate a joint at the other end
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The radius and ulna form a ring connected by the proximal and distal radioulnar joints, so a displaced single-bone fracture usually dislocates a joint at the other end.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A 20-year-old falls onto his shoulder playing rugby and presents supporting his arm against his body with his head tilted toward the injured side, and a visible lump over the collarbone. Where is the fracture most likely located?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The middle third
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: About 80% of clavicle fractures occur in the middle third (the thinnest, least-supported part); the described posture and lump are classic.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What proportion of clavicle fractures occur in the middle third?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: About 80%
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Approximately 80% of clavicle fractures occur in the middle third.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which clavicle fracture location has the highest non-union risk and is more often managed surgically?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Lateral (distal) third
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Lateral (distal) third fractures (~15%) have a higher non-union risk and are more often treated surgically.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A medial-third clavicle fracture from high-energy trauma should prompt assessment for which associated injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Intra-thoracic/great-vessel injury and pneumothorax
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Medial-third/high-energy clavicle fractures can be associated with intra-thoracic/great-vessel injury and pneumothorax (the lung apex lies beneath).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which neurovascular structures lie just deep to the clavicle and must be assessed?
options: The median nerve and radial artery
The sciatic nerve and popliteal artery
The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The subclavian vessels and brachial plexus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The subclavian artery/vein and brachial plexus run just deep to the clavicle, so distal pulses/perfusion and limb neurology must be checked.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the standard management of a minimally displaced middle-third clavicle fracture?
options: A broad arm sling, analgesia and early mobilisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: A broad arm sling, analgesia and early mobilisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Most middle-third minimally displaced fractures are managed conservatively with a sling, analgesia and early mobilisation, healing well.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgical fixation of a clavicle fracture?
options: An open fracture or threatened/tented skin, neurovascular injury, or significant displacement/shortening (>2 cm)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An open fracture or threatened/tented skin, neurovascular injury, or significant displacement/shortening (>2 cm)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Surgery (ORIF) is indicated for open fractures, threatened skin, neurovascular injury, significant displacement/shortening (>2 cm)/comminution, displaced lateral-third fractures or non-union.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: How does the medial fragment displace in a mid-clavicle fracture, and why?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Upward, pulled by sternocleidomastoid
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The medial fragment is pulled upward by sternocleidomastoid, while the lateral fragment is pulled down/medially by arm weight and pectoralis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: How is a neonatal clavicle fracture (e.g. from shoulder dystocia) managed?
options: Gentle handling — it heals rapidly with minimal/no intervention
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Gentle handling — it heals rapidly with minimal/no intervention
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Neonatal clavicle fractures heal rapidly with minimal/no intervention and have a good prognosis (gentle handling).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A collision-sport athlete falls onto the point of the shoulder and has a step deformity at the top of the shoulder with intact clavicle bone. What is the likely injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury ('shoulder separation')
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A fall onto the point of the shoulder disrupting the AC joint/ligaments is an AC joint injury (shoulder separation), distinct from a clavicle fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: How is a grade 1 or 2 acromioclavicular joint injury managed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Conservative — rest and a sling
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: AC joint injuries of grades 1–2 are managed conservatively with rest and a sling; grade 3 is either, and grades 4–6 need surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which imaging is appropriate for a suspected medial-third clavicle fracture with possible chest involvement?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: CT (± CXR if pneumothorax suspected)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Medial-third fractures or suspected intra-thoracic/sternoclavicular injury warrant CT, with a CXR if a pneumothorax is suspected.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is a recognised complication of a displaced or lateral-third clavicle fracture?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Non-union/malunion
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Non-union/malunion (especially with displaced or lateral-third fractures) is a recognised complication, along with a persistent lump and rarely neurovascular injury/pneumothorax.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A clavicle fracture patient has tented, blanching skin over the fracture. What does this indicate?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Threatened skin — a surgical urgency
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Tented/threatened skin risks becoming an open fracture and is a surgical urgency requiring fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the key difference between a clavicle fracture and an AC joint injury?
options: A clavicle fracture never needs a sling
A clavicle fracture is a break in the bone; an AC joint injury is disruption of the acromioclavicular joint/ligaments
An AC joint injury is always surgical
A clavicle fracture only occurs in children
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: A clavicle fracture is a break in the bone; an AC joint injury is disruption of the acromioclavicular joint/ligaments
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A clavicle fracture is a bony break, whereas an AC joint injury ('separation') is disruption of the acromioclavicular joint and its ligaments.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Early shoulder mobilisation (pendulum exercises) is encouraged in clavicle fractures once comfortable in order to:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Prevent shoulder stiffness
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Early mobilisation once comfortable prevents shoulder stiffness while the fracture heals in the sling.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A 40-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and has lateral elbow pain with painful, restricted forearm rotation. X-ray shows a subtle undisplaced fracture with a posterior fat pad sign. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Radial head fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Lateral elbow pain with restricted forearm rotation after a FOOSH, plus a fat pad sign, is a radial head fracture — the commonest elbow fracture in adults.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is the commonest elbow fracture in ADULTS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Radial head fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The radial head fracture is the commonest elbow fracture in adults, typically from a FOOSH.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which functional sign is key in a radial head fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Painful and restricted forearm rotation (supination/pronation)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The radial head is central to forearm rotation, so painful/restricted supination/pronation is the key functional sign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What does ANY posterior fat pad sign on an elbow X-ray indicate?
options: An intra-articular fracture (often an occult radial head fracture)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An intra-articular fracture (often an occult radial head fracture)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Any posterior fat pad is abnormal and indicates an intra-articular fracture — often the only sign of an occult, undisplaced radial head fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: According to the Mason classification, how is a Mason I (undisplaced) radial head fracture managed?
options: Conservative — brief sling then EARLY mobilisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Conservative — brief sling then EARLY mobilisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Mason I (undisplaced) fractures are managed conservatively with a brief sling and early mobilisation to avoid stiffness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which is a key SURGICAL indication in a radial head fracture?
options: A mechanical block to forearm rotation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: A mechanical block to forearm rotation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A mechanical block to forearm rotation is a key surgical indication; aspiration + local anaesthetic helps distinguish a mechanical from a painful block.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A comminuted, unreconstructable radial head fracture (Mason III) in an unstable elbow is best managed by:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Radial head replacement (a key stabiliser)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: For a comminuted (Mason III) fracture with elbow instability, radial head replacement is preferred, as the radial head is a key elbow stabiliser.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A radial head fracture with interosseous membrane disruption and a DRUJ dislocation (wrist pain) is called:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: An Essex-Lopresti injury
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: An Essex-Lopresti injury is a radial head fracture with interosseous membrane disruption and DRUJ dislocation — so the wrist must be checked.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the 'terrible triad' of the elbow?
options: Radial head + olecranon + medial epicondyle fractures
Elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture
Radial head + DRUJ + interosseous membrane injury
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Elbow dislocation + radial head fracture + coronoid fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The terrible triad is elbow dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures — an unstable pattern requiring surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the COMMONEST complication of a radial head fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Elbow stiffness / loss of extension
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Elbow stiffness/loss of extension is the commonest complication, which is why early mobilisation is emphasised.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which nerve should be assessed in a radial head fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The posterior interosseous nerve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve should be assessed in a radial head fracture (test finger/thumb extension).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Which imaging is used for a comminuted radial head fracture and surgical planning?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: CT
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: CT is used for comminuted radial head fractures and surgical planning, in addition to plain X-ray.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: What is the anterior fat pad sign in a radial head fracture also called?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: The sail sign
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The anterior fat pad, lifted by an effusion, produces a 'sail sign'; any posterior fat pad is abnormal.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why must the wrist be examined in a radial head fracture?
options: To check for a scaphoid fracture only
To detect an Essex-Lopresti injury (DRUJ dislocation/interosseous membrane disruption)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: To detect an Essex-Lopresti injury (DRUJ dislocation/interosseous membrane disruption)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: Examining the wrist detects an Essex-Lopresti injury (interosseous membrane disruption + DRUJ dislocation), which can be missed with chronic consequences.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: A Mason II radial head fracture is displaced with a mechanical block to rotation. What is the appropriate management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: ORIF (screws/plate)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: A displaced Mason II fracture with a mechanical block is managed with ORIF (screws/plate); undisplaced ones without a block are treated conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.question: Why is early active mobilisation preferred for an undisplaced radial head fracture?
options: Because the elbow is very prone to stiffness/contracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.answer: Because the elbow is very prone to stiffness/contracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Upper Limb Fra.explanation: The elbow stiffens easily, so early active mobilisation (within days) preserves range in undisplaced (Mason I) fractures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 60-year-old tennis player has shoulder pain, weakness on abduction and difficulty sleeping on that side. The empty-can (Jobe's) test is positive. Which tendon is most likely affected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Weak abduction with a positive empty-can (Jobe's) test localises to the supraspinatus — the most commonly affected cuff tendon.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which pattern of movement restriction suggests a rotator cuff problem rather than a frozen shoulder?
options: Loss of both active and passive movement
Loss of passive external rotation only
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Rotator cuff disease limits active movement more than passive; frozen shoulder loses both active and passive movement (especially external rotation).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What do the SITS muscles stand for?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: SITS = Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Teres minor and Subscapularis — the rotator cuff muscles.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates the first ~15° of abduction?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The supraspinatus initiates abduction (the first ~15°); the deltoid takes over thereafter.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Weakness of external rotation points to which rotator cuff tendon(s)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: External rotation is produced by the infraspinatus and teres minor, so weakness there localises the tear to those tendons.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which test assesses the subscapularis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Gerber's lift-off test (lifting the hand off the lower back against resistance) assesses the subscapularis (internal rotation).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A painful arc through 60–120° of abduction most suggests:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A painful arc at 60–120° of abduction suggests subacromial impingement/supraspinatus involvement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which is the most commonly torn rotator cuff tendon, and why?
options: Teres minor, because it is weakest
Supraspinatus, because it passes under the acromion and is most prone to impingement
Infraspinatus, because it is most superficial
Deltoid, because it is most used
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Supraspinatus, because it passes under the acromion and is most prone to impingement
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The supraspinatus is most commonly torn because it passes under the acromion and is most prone to subacromial impingement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the first-line imaging investigation for rotator cuff disorders?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Ultrasound is first-line — a dynamic assessment of the cuff tendons that detects and sizes tears; MRI is used for full-thickness tears/surgical planning.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 68-year-old with a degenerative partial-thickness rotator cuff tear has pain and mild weakness. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Conservative — rest, analgesia and physiotherapy (± subacromial steroid injection)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Conservative — rest, analgesia and physiotherapy (± subacromial steroid injection)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Degenerative cuff disease is managed conservatively — rest/activity modification, analgesia and physiotherapy (the cornerstone), ± a subacromial steroid injection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 35-year-old sustains an acute traumatic full-thickness supraspinatus tear with marked weakness. What is the most appropriate management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Acute full-thickness tears in young, active, high-demand patients are managed with arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (tendon reattached to bone).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which symptom is classically associated with rotator cuff disease at night?
options: Difficulty sleeping — unable to lie on the affected shoulder
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Difficulty sleeping — unable to lie on the affected shoulder
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Night pain with difficulty sleeping (unable to lie on the affected shoulder) is a classic feature of rotator cuff disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: The empty-can (Jobe's) test specifically assesses which tendon?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The empty-can (Jobe's) test — resisted abduction in the empty-can position — assesses the supraspinatus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: An X-ray in chronic rotator cuff disease shows a high-riding humeral head. What does this suggest?
options: A large chronic rotator cuff tear
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: A large chronic rotator cuff tear
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A high-riding humeral head on X-ray suggests a large chronic rotator cuff tear (the head migrates superiorly without cuff restraint).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which is the cornerstone of conservative rotator cuff management?
options: Physiotherapy (strengthening the cuff and scapular stabilisers, restoring range)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Physiotherapy (strengthening the cuff and scapular stabilisers, restoring range)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Physiotherapy — strengthening the cuff and scapular stabilisers and restoring range — is the cornerstone of conservative management.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Loss of BOTH active and passive shoulder movement, especially external rotation, points to which condition rather than a rotator cuff tear?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Loss of both active and passive movement (especially external rotation) indicates a capsular problem — frozen shoulder — not a cuff tear.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A patient presents with a sudden pop in the arm and a 'Popeye' bulge of the muscle belly. Which shoulder disorder is this?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A sudden pop with a 'Popeye' deformity (bunched-up muscle belly) is a biceps tendon rupture, usually managed conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which subacromial injection is used adjunctively for painful degenerative rotator cuff disease/impingement?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A subacromial corticosteroid injection can be used adjunctively for pain/impingement in degenerative rotator cuff disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Why is frozen shoulder important to consider in a patient with global shoulder stiffness?
options: It is strongly associated with diabetes — check glucose
It never causes external rotation loss
It is caused by a full-thickness tear
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: It is strongly associated with diabetes — check glucose
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Frozen shoulder is strongly associated with diabetes, so glucose should be checked; it causes global stiffness with external rotation most affected.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which combination best fits rotator cuff disease?
options: Shoulder pain, weakness on specific movements localising the tendon, and night pain
Loss of passive external rotation with normal strength
A sudden pop with a muscle bulge
Fever and a hot swollen joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Shoulder pain, weakness on specific movements localising the tendon, and night pain
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Shoulder pain with weakness on specific movements (localising the affected tendon) and night pain is the classic picture of rotator cuff disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has 6 months of progressive shoulder pain and stiffness. On examination, both active AND passive movement are restricted, especially external rotation. The X-ray is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Restriction of both active and passive movement (especially external rotation) with a normal X-ray, in a diabetic middle-aged woman, is frozen shoulder.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the defining examination finding of frozen shoulder?
options: Both active AND passive movement are restricted (a tight capsule)
Only external rotation strength is reduced
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Both active AND passive movement are restricted (a tight capsule)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Frozen shoulder restricts both active and passive movement because the capsule is physically tight — unlike a cuff tear, where passive range is preserved.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which movement is most affected in frozen shoulder?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: External rotation is the most affected movement in frozen shoulder.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the KEY risk factor for frozen shoulder?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Diabetes mellitus is the strongest risk factor and is often associated with more severe/bilateral disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What underlies frozen shoulder pathologically?
options: Inflammation and fibrosis of the joint capsule with adhesions
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Inflammation and fibrosis of the joint capsule with adhesions
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Frozen shoulder is inflammation then fibrosis of the glenohumeral capsule, forming adhesions that bind and tighten it.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What are the three phases of frozen shoulder, in order?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The course is painful → stiff (frozen) → thawing, over 1–3 years.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Over what timescale does frozen shoulder typically resolve?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Frozen shoulder is self-limiting but slow, running its course over 1–3 years (up to 50% have persistent symptoms).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What should the X-ray show in frozen shoulder?
options: A normal appearance (it is used to exclude osteoarthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: A normal appearance (it is used to exclude osteoarthritis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The X-ray in frozen shoulder is normal — it is used to exclude osteoarthritis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: How does frozen shoulder differ from a rotator cuff tear on examination?
options: A cuff tear restricts passive movement more
Frozen shoulder has normal active range
Frozen shoulder restricts passive movement, whereas a cuff tear preserves passive range (only active limited)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Frozen shoulder restricts passive movement, whereas a cuff tear preserves passive range (only active limited)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: In frozen shoulder passive movement is restricted (tight capsule), whereas in a cuff tear passive range is preserved and only active movement is limited by weakness.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the overall management approach to frozen shoulder?
options: A single curative operation for all
Symptomatic management (analgesia, physiotherapy, steroids) while it runs its course, with surgery for refractory cases
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Symptomatic management (analgesia, physiotherapy, steroids) while it runs its course, with surgery for refractory cases
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: No single intervention clearly changes the natural history, so management is symptomatic and supportive, reserving MUA/capsular release for refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which treatment is particularly useful in the early/painful phase of frozen shoulder?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: NSAIDs and corticosteroids (oral or intra-articular) help control pain and inflammation, especially early in the painful phase.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What surgical option is used for refractory frozen shoulder?
options: Manipulation under anaesthesia (± arthroscopic capsular release)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Manipulation under anaesthesia (± arthroscopic capsular release)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Manipulation under anaesthesia — forcefully stretching the capsule to break adhesions — ± arthroscopic capsular release is reserved for refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Besides shoulder-directed treatment, what should be optimised in a diabetic patient with frozen shoulder?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Optimising diabetes control is important, as diabetes is the key risk factor for frozen shoulder.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A patient's shoulder pain has settled but marked stiffness now dominates, limiting all movement. Which phase of frozen shoulder is this?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: When pain settles but stiffness predominates and limits movement, the patient is in the stiff (frozen) phase.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for frozen shoulder besides diabetes?
options: Thyroid disease, prolonged immobilisation or previous shoulder injury/surgery
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Thyroid disease, prolonged immobilisation or previous shoulder injury/surgery
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Thyroid disease, prolonged immobilisation, previous shoulder injury/surgery and Dupuytren's are recognised risk factors, along with middle-aged female sex.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Imaging with ultrasound or MRI in frozen shoulder characteristically shows:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Ultrasound/MRI shows a thickened joint capsule, supporting the diagnosis of frozen shoulder if imaging is needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 45-year-old man feels a sudden pop in the front of his shoulder while doing pull-ups, followed by a bulge in the middle of his upper arm. He has minimal weakness. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Proximal (long head) biceps rupture — conservative management
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Proximal (long head) biceps rupture — conservative management
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A pop at the shoulder with a Popeye deformity and minimal functional loss is a proximal (long head) biceps rupture, managed conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which biceps tendon ruptures most commonly?
options: The short head at the origin
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The proximal long head of biceps is by far the commonest rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A 50-year-old feels a pop at the front of the elbow (antecubital fossa) after his flexed arm was forcefully straightened, and now has weak supination. What is the diagnosis and management?
options: Distal biceps rupture — prompt surgical repair
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Distal biceps rupture — prompt surgical repair
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A pop at the antecubital fossa with significant supination weakness is a distal biceps rupture, which needs prompt surgical repair.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the Popeye deformity, and which rupture produces it?
options: A bulge at the elbow from a distal rupture
A bulge in the mid-upper arm from a proximal (long head) rupture
A step deformity at the AC joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: A bulge in the mid-upper arm from a proximal (long head) rupture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The Popeye deformity is a bulge of the retracted muscle belly in the mid-upper arm, classic for a proximal (long head) rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Why does a proximal long head biceps rupture cause minimal functional loss?
options: The biceps is not a functional muscle
The short head and brachialis compensate
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: The short head and brachialis compensate
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The short head of biceps and brachialis compensate, so a proximal long head rupture causes minimal functional loss (mainly cosmetic).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which movement is particularly weakened by a distal biceps rupture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The biceps is the main forearm supinator, so a distal rupture notably weakens supination (and elbow flexion).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the mechanism of a distal biceps rupture?
options: A direct blow to the shoulder
A fall on an outstretched hand
A flexed elbow suddenly and forcefully extended while the biceps is contracted (eccentric overload)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: A flexed elbow suddenly and forcefully extended while the biceps is contracted (eccentric overload)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A distal rupture occurs when a flexed, contracting elbow is suddenly forcefully extended — an eccentric overload.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which test helps confirm biceps tendon integrity, analogous to the Achilles calf-squeeze test?
options: The biceps squeeze test (intact tendon → forearm supination)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: The biceps squeeze test (intact tendon → forearm supination)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: The biceps squeeze test: squeezing the muscle belly produces supination if the tendon is intact; no supination suggests a distal rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: What is the first-line imaging investigation for a suspected biceps rupture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: MSK ultrasound is first-line, confirming the rupture and its location; urgent MRI is used for suspected distal ruptures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Which risk factor predisposes to biceps tendon rupture?
options: Corticosteroid use, smoking, overhead overuse and increasing age
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Corticosteroid use, smoking, overhead overuse and increasing age
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Corticosteroids, smoking, overhead/shoulder overuse and increasing age make the tendon degenerate, predisposing to rupture with modest force.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: How is a proximal (long head) biceps rupture managed?
options: Conservative management — analgesia, rest and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Conservative management — analgesia, rest and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A proximal long head rupture is managed conservatively (analgesia, rest, physiotherapy), as the Popeye deformity is mostly cosmetic and function is preserved.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: Why should a distal biceps rupture be repaired promptly (within ~2–3 weeks)?
options: Because the tendon retracts and scars, making late repair harder and recovery poorer
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.answer: Because the tendon retracts and scars, making late repair harder and recovery poorer
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: A distal tendon retracts and scars over time, so prompt repair (within ~2–3 weeks) gives better results than delayed surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.question: A patient with a suspected distal biceps rupture needs which urgent investigation to plan surgery?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Shoulder Disor.explanation: Urgent MRI best defines a distal biceps tear, which needs prompt surgical repair.
