conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: A hinged knee brace with protected/non-weight-bearing, then graded weight-bearing and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: Undisplaced/minimally depressed stable fractures are managed non-operatively with a hinged brace and protected weight-bearing progressing to graded weight-bearing.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: What does ORIF of a depressed tibial plateau fracture typically involve?
options: Elevating the depressed fragment, bone grafting the defect, and stabilising with plates/screws to restore a congruent joint surface
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: Elevating the depressed fragment, bone grafting the defect, and stabilising with plates/screws to restore a congruent joint surface
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: ORIF elevates the depressed fragment, bone grafts the defect and stabilises with plates/screws to restore a congruent articular surface.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: A high-energy tibial plateau fracture is confirmed to have a popliteal artery injury. What is the appropriate management of this associated injury?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: Urgent revascularisation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: A vascular (popliteal artery) injury requires urgent revascularisation; associated compartment syndrome needs fasciotomy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: Which imaging finding on plain X-ray supports an intra-articular tibial plateau fracture?
options: A joint effusion with no fat level
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: A lipohaemarthrosis (fat-fluid level)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: A fat-fluid level (lipohaemarthrosis) on X-ray reflects marrow fat in the joint, supporting an intra-articular fracture such as a tibial plateau fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: Which patient/mechanism is typical of a LOW-energy tibial plateau fracture?
options: A young adult in a high-speed car crash
An osteoporotic elderly patient after a simple fall
A pedestrian struck by a car
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: An osteoporotic elderly patient after a simple fall
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: Low-energy plateau fractures (simple depression/split) typically occur in osteoporotic elderly patients after a simple fall; high-energy fractures occur in younger patients.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: What is the correct imaging sequence for a tibial plateau fracture?
options: CT angiography first in all patients
X-ray → CT (define the articular surface, plan surgery) → MRI for soft tissues
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: X-ray → CT (define the articular surface, plan surgery) → MRI for soft tissues
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: The sequence is X-ray first, then CT to define the articular surface and plan surgery, with MRI for associated ligament/meniscal injuries (CT angiography if vascular injury is suspected).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.question: Which associated injuries are commonly seen with tibial plateau fractures because of the mechanism?
options: Ligament and meniscal injuries, plus neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.answer: Ligament and meniscal injuries, plus neurovascular injury and compartment syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Limb Fra.explanation: The axial ± valgus/varus mechanism frequently damages ligaments, menisci, the popliteal artery and peroneal nerve, and swelling risks compartment syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 35-year-old warehouse worker has lower back pain that came on after lifting, is worse with movement and better with rest, with no leg symptoms, no systemic features and a normal neurological examination. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent MRI of the lumbar spine
Reassurance, stay active, and NSAIDs (with a PPI if over 45)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Reassurance, stay active, and NSAIDs (with a PPI if over 45)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: This is benign mechanical back pain with no red flags — manage with reassurance, staying active and NSAIDs; routine imaging is not indicated.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which combination of symptoms should prompt an EMERGENCY MRI for suspected cauda equina syndrome?
options: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica
Unilateral leg pain with a positive straight-leg raise
Back pain worse on standing, relieved by sitting
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica indicate cauda equina syndrome — an emergency requiring urgent MRI and decompression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Approximately what proportion of back pain is mechanical (non-specific)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: More than 90%
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: More than 90% of back pain is benign mechanical/non-specific pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 68-year-old with a history of breast cancer develops new back pain that is worse at night and associated with weight loss. What do these red flags most suggest?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Malignancy / metastatic spinal cord compression
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Age >50, previous cancer, night pain and weight loss are red flags pointing to malignancy/metastatic spinal cord compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: According to NICE, what is the first-line analgesia for low back pain?
options: An NSAID (e.g. naproxen), with a PPI in the over-45s
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: An NSAID (e.g. naproxen), with a PPI in the over-45s
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: NICE recommends an NSAID first-line (co-prescribing a PPI in over-45s); paracetamol alone, strong opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids are not recommended.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which of the following does NICE advise AGAINST for non-specific low back pain?
options: NSAIDs with a PPI where appropriate
Routinely offering paracetamol alone or using strong opioids/gabapentinoids
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Routinely offering paracetamol alone or using strong opioids/gabapentinoids
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: NICE advises against routinely offering paracetamol alone and against strong opioids, benzodiazepines and gabapentinoids for low back pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A young man reports back pain and stiffness that is worst in the morning and improves with exercise through the day. Which diagnosis should this pattern prompt, rather than mechanical back pain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Ankylosing spondylitis (inflammatory back pain)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Morning stiffness that improves with movement in a young patient is an inflammatory back pain pattern suggesting ankylosing spondylitis, not mechanical pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which advice about activity is correct for mechanical back pain?
options: Strict bed rest for at least a week
Immobilise the spine in a brace
Stay active and continue normal activities; avoid bed rest
Bed rest until an MRI is done
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Stay active and continue normal activities; avoid bed rest
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Staying active and avoiding bed rest is the cornerstone — bed rest worsens outcomes in mechanical back pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient presents with fever, raised inflammatory markers and focal spinal tenderness, and is an IV drug user. Which serious cause of back pain is most likely?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Spinal infection (discitis/epidural abscess)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Fever, systemic illness, raised inflammatory markers and IV drug use point to spinal infection (discitis/epidural abscess).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which patient with back pain does NOT require imaging?
options: A 30-year-old with movement-related back pain, no red flags and normal neurology
A 70-year-old with night pain and weight loss
A patient with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention
A febrile IV drug user with focal spinal tenderness
A patient with a positive straight-leg raise and progressive foot drop
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A 30-year-old with movement-related back pain, no red flags and normal neurology
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Benign mechanical back pain without red flags or neurological deficit does not require routine imaging.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which set of features best fits BENIGN mechanical back pain?
options: Night pain, weight loss and previous cancer
Saddle anaesthesia and bilateral leg symptoms
Pain varying with posture/movement, no systemic features and normal neurology
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Pain varying with posture/movement, no systemic features and normal neurology
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Mechanical back pain varies with posture/movement, has no systemic features and a normal neurological examination.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 74-year-old woman on long-term steroids develops sudden severe back pain after a minor stumble. Which red-flag cause is most likely?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: An osteoporotic vertebral (fragility) fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Trauma (even minor), osteoporosis and steroid use are red flags for a vertebral fragility fracture, which classically causes acute pain after minimal stress.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the urgent treatment pathway for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Dexamethasone + urgent MRI + oncology referral
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Suspected MSCC requires dexamethasone, urgent whole-spine MRI and oncology referral to guide radiotherapy/surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which finding indicates SCIATICA (radiculopathy) rather than simple mechanical back pain?
options: Pain confined to the lower back, worse on movement
Pain relieved only by lying flat
Pain radiating down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern with a positive straight-leg raise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Pain radiating down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern with a positive straight-leg raise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Dermatomal leg pain below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise indicates nerve root compression (sciatica).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which pattern is characteristic of lumbar spinal stenosis?
options: Leg pain at rest relieved by standing
Neurogenic claudication — leg pain on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting
Pain only at night with weight loss
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Neurogenic claudication — leg pain on walking, relieved by flexion/sitting
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication — leg pain brought on by walking and relieved by lumbar flexion/sitting.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with mechanical back pain is over 45 and needs an NSAID. What co-prescription does NICE advise?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A proton pump inhibitor (PPI)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: NICE advises co-prescribing a PPI with NSAIDs in the over-45s for gastroprotection.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which blood tests are appropriate when malignancy or infection is suspected as a cause of back pain?
options: No blood tests are ever useful
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: FBC, CRP/ESR ± myeloma screen / PSA
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: If a serious cause is suspected, FBC, CRP/ESR and (as relevant) a myeloma screen or PSA are appropriate, alongside MRI.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Why is routine X-ray/MRI unhelpful in simple mechanical back pain?
options: It exposes the patient to radiation (X-ray) and often reveals incidental findings without changing management
It is only available in emergencies
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: It exposes the patient to radiation (X-ray) and often reveals incidental findings without changing management
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Routine imaging of simple back pain adds radiation (X-ray) and frequently shows incidental degenerative findings that do not change management — reserve it for red flags.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 55-year-old presents with back pain but no red flags, normal neurology and pain clearly related to movement. What is the single best next step?
options: Advise two weeks of bed rest
Reassurance, advice to stay active, and NSAIDs
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Reassurance, advice to stay active, and NSAIDs
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: With no red flags and normal neurology, manage conservatively — reassurance, staying active and NSAIDs — without imaging.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the definitive management of cauda equina syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Emergency surgical decompression (after urgent MRI)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome requires emergency MRI and surgical decompression to prevent permanent bladder/bowel and neurological damage.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 40-year-old develops sharp pain radiating from the buttock down the back of the leg to the lateral foot and small toe, with a reduced ankle jerk. Which nerve root is most likely affected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: S1
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Lateral foot/small toe sensory loss with a reduced ankle jerk indicates an S1 root lesion (weak plantarflexion/eversion).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with sciatica has weakness of big-toe and foot dorsiflexion (foot drop) and sensory loss over the big toe and dorsum of the foot, with normal reflexes. Which root is affected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: L5
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Big toe/dorsum of foot sensory loss with foot drop and no reflex change is an L5 root lesion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the commonest cause of sciatica, and at which levels does it typically occur?
options: A prolapsed intervertebral disc, at L4/5 or L5/S1
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A prolapsed intervertebral disc, at L4/5 or L5/S1
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: A prolapsed (herniated) disc, usually at L4/5 or L5/S1, is the commonest cause of sciatica.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which test reproduces radicular pain by stretching the nerve root and is positive in L5/S1 radiculopathy?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: The straight leg raise (SLR)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: The straight leg raise reproduces the radicular pain by stretching the L5/S1 nerve roots — a positive result supports sciatica.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: According to NICE, what is the recommended drug management of sciatica?
options: The same as for back pain without sciatica — NSAIDs (± PPI) first-line
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: The same as for back pain without sciatica — NSAIDs (± PPI) first-line
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: NICE advises using the same drugs as for back pain — NSAIDs first-line (± PPI) — and NOT neuropathic agents (gabapentin/pregabalin/duloxetine) for sciatica.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which combination of symptoms in a patient with sciatica indicates cauda equina syndrome requiring emergency MRI?
options: Unilateral leg pain with a positive SLR
Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica with reduced anal tone
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction and bilateral sciatica with reduced anal tone
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica and reduced anal tone indicate cauda equina syndrome — an emergency.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: When should MRI be performed in a patient with uncomplicated sciatica?
options: Only if symptoms persist beyond about 4–6 weeks (or urgently if red flags)
At first presentation in all patients
Only if the SLR is negative
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Only if symptoms persist beyond about 4–6 weeks (or urgently if red flags)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Most sciatica resolves, so MRI is reserved for symptoms persisting beyond ~4–6 weeks, or urgently when red flags (e.g. cauda equina) are present.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: The pain of true sciatica characteristically:
options: Stays in the lower back only
Is symmetrical across the whole back
Radiates down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern
Is worse on standing and relieved by sitting
Improves with rest and worsens with movement only
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Radiates down the leg below the knee in a dermatomal pattern
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: True sciatica radiates below the knee in a nerve-root (dermatomal) distribution and is usually worse than the back pain, often worse on sitting.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which reflex is lost in an S1 radiculopathy?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: The ankle jerk
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: The ankle jerk (S1/2 — 'buckle my shoe') is lost in an S1 radiculopathy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with confirmed L5/S1 disc prolapse has severe radicular pain persisting despite 8 weeks of NSAIDs, physiotherapy and staying active. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Specialist referral for MRI, with consideration of epidural injection or microdiscectomy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Specialist referral for MRI, with consideration of epidural injection or microdiscectomy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Persistent/severe radicular pain beyond ~4–6 weeks warrants MRI and specialist referral, with epidural corticosteroid injection or microdiscectomy for refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which of the following patients needs URGENT surgery?
options: A patient with sciatica improving on NSAIDs
A patient with a positive SLR and mild pain
A patient with back pain only
A patient with progressive motor weakness or cauda equina syndrome
A patient whose leg pain is worse on sitting
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A patient with progressive motor weakness or cauda equina syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Progressive motor weakness or cauda equina syndrome requires urgent surgical decompression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which management advice is correct for most patients with sciatica?
options: Reassurance, stay active and physiotherapy with NSAIDs, as most resolve within weeks
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Reassurance, stay active and physiotherapy with NSAIDs, as most resolve within weeks
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Most sciatica is self-limiting — manage with reassurance, staying active, physiotherapy and NSAIDs; avoid bed rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient has sensory loss over the medial shin and ankle with weak knee extension and dorsiflexion, and a reduced knee jerk. Which root is most likely affected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: L4
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Medial shin/ankle sensory loss with weak knee extension/dorsiflexion and a reduced knee jerk indicates an L4 root lesion (knee reflex is L3/4).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which statement about the location of a disc herniation causing sciatica is correct?
options: It never compresses a nerve root
It only occurs in the cervical spine
It compresses the spinal cord at L5/S1
It usually herniates posterolaterally, compressing the adjacent nerve root
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: It usually herniates posterolaterally, compressing the adjacent nerve root
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Disc herniation is usually posterolateral, compressing the adjacent lumbosacral nerve root and producing radicular symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Why are neuropathic agents (e.g. gabapentin) no longer recommended for sciatica by NICE?
options: Evidence does not support them for sciatica, which should be managed like ordinary back pain (NSAIDs first-line)
They only work for cervical radiculopathy
They are contraindicated in all back pain
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Evidence does not support them for sciatica, which should be managed like ordinary back pain (NSAIDs first-line)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: NICE recommends managing sciatica with the same approach as back pain (NSAIDs ± PPI first-line); gabapentinoids/duloxetine are no longer recommended for sciatica.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which examination sequence best localises the affected root in sciatica?
options: Assessing the dermatome, reflex, myotome and straight leg raise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Assessing the dermatome, reflex, myotome and straight leg raise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Localising the root relies on the dermatome (sensation), reflex, myotome (power) and SLR — the core neurological assessment in sciatica.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient reports leg pain worse than their back pain, worse when sitting, radiating to the big toe, with weak great-toe dorsiflexion. Which single root is implicated?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: L5
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Pain radiating to the big toe with weak great-toe dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus) localises to the L5 root.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 70-year-old man reports bilateral leg heaviness and pain when walking that is relieved by sitting or leaning forward on his shopping trolley. He can walk uphill more easily than downhill, and his foot pulses are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sciatica from a single disc prolapse
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Neurogenic claudication relieved by flexion/sitting, easier uphill, with normal pulses is classic lumbar spinal stenosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which feature best distinguishes neurogenic from vascular claudication?
options: Both are relieved by rest equally
Neurogenic is relieved by sitting/bending forward with normal pulses; vascular is relieved by standing/rest with reduced pulses and low ABPI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Neurogenic is relieved by sitting/bending forward with normal pulses; vascular is relieved by standing/rest with reduced pulses and low ABPI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Neurogenic claudication is relieved by flexion/sitting with normal pulses; vascular claudication is relieved by rest/standing with reduced pulses and a low ABPI.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the 'uphill paradox' in lumbar spinal stenosis?
options: Walking uphill is easier because the forward-flexed posture opens the canal
Walking uphill worsens the pain due to muscle demand
Uphill walking causes pulses to disappear
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Walking uphill is easier because the forward-flexed posture opens the canal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: In stenosis, the forward-flexed posture of walking uphill opens the canal, making it easier — the opposite of vascular claudication (worse uphill).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the commonest cause of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Degenerative (age-related) canal narrowing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Age-related degenerative change (facet hypertrophy, ligamentum flavum thickening, disc bulging, osteophytes) is the commonest cause.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which posture or activity RELIEVES the symptoms of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Sitting or bending forward
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Flexion (sitting or bending forward) opens the narrowed canal and relieves the neurogenic claudication.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which investigation is the imaging of choice for lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: MRI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: MRI is the imaging of choice, demonstrating the level, degree and cause of canal narrowing.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which bedside assessment helps exclude vascular claudication in a patient with suspected spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Peripheral pulses and ABPI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Checking peripheral pulses and the ABPI distinguishes vascular claudication (reduced) from neurogenic claudication (normal).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the first-line management of lumbar spinal stenosis?
options: Conservative — analgesia, physiotherapy and flexion-based exercise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Conservative — analgesia, physiotherapy and flexion-based exercise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Conservative management (analgesia, physiotherapy/flexion-based exercise, activity modification, weight loss) is first-line.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the surgical treatment for severe or refractory lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Decompressive laminectomy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Decompressive laminectomy widens the canal (removing lamina ± ligamentum flavum/osteophytes) and is used for severe/refractory symptoms or significant neurological compromise.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which type of exercise is preferred in lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Flexion-based exercise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Flexion-based exercise is preferred because spinal flexion opens the narrowed canal and relieves symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with vascular claudication would be expected to have which finding, unlike neurogenic claudication?
options: Reduced/absent foot pulses and a low ABPI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Reduced/absent foot pulses and a low ABPI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Vascular claudication is characterised by reduced/absent pulses and a low ABPI, whereas neurogenic claudication has normal pulses.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which serious complication must be screened for in severe central lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Cauda equina syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Severe central stenosis can compress the cauda equina, so cauda equina syndrome must be screened for.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: How quickly do symptoms typically ease on stopping in neurogenic versus vascular claudication?
options: Neurogenic eases quickly; vascular is slow
Neurogenic is slower to ease (minutes); vascular eases quickly with rest
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Neurogenic is slower to ease (minutes); vascular eases quickly with rest
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Neurogenic claudication is slower to settle (over minutes, often needing to sit/flex), whereas vascular claudication eases quickly with rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which of the following is a recognised, less common cause of lumbar spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Paget's disease of bone
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Besides degeneration, causes include disc prolapse, tumour, spondylolisthesis, a congenitally narrow canal and Paget's disease of bone.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient describes leg pain on walking that is worse going uphill and eases quickly when they stop and stand still; their foot is cold with absent pulses. Which diagnosis is this, rather than spinal stenosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Vascular (peripheral arterial) claudication
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Worse uphill, quick relief on standing/rest, a cold foot and absent pulses indicate vascular claudication, not neurogenic claudication.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which combination is most characteristic of lumbar spinal stenosis?
options: Young patient, unilateral pain below the knee, positive SLR
Older patient, bilateral leg pain/heaviness on walking relieved by sitting/flexion, easier uphill
Sudden pain after minor trauma with a wedge fracture
Morning stiffness improving with movement in a young man
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Older patient, bilateral leg pain/heaviness on walking relieved by sitting/flexion, easier uphill
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: An older patient with bilateral neurogenic claudication relieved by sitting/bending forward and easier uphill is the classic picture of lumbar spinal stenosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: An IV drug user presents with severe, unremitting night-time back pain, fever and rigors, and new weakness in the legs. Inflammatory markers are markedly raised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Discitis (spinal infection)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Severe back pain with systemic sepsis and new neurology in an IV drug user is discitis until proven otherwise — urgent MRI and blood cultures are needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the commonest causative organism of discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Staphylococcus aureus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest organism causing discitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which investigation is the MOST sensitive for diagnosing discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: MRI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: MRI is the most sensitive investigation, showing disc-space infection, surrounding inflammation and any epidural abscess/cord compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Because discitis is usually haematogenous, which source should always be actively sought?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Infective endocarditis (via echocardiography)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Discitis usually spreads haematogenously, so echocardiography (TTE/TOE) is performed to assess for infective endocarditis as the source.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which triad is characteristic of discitis?
options: Back pain, weight loss and night sweats
Claudication, normal pulses and relief on sitting
Severe back pain, systemic sepsis (fever/rigors) and neurological symptoms
Morning stiffness, young age and improvement with movement
Sudden pain, minor trauma and a wedge fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Severe back pain, systemic sepsis (fever/rigors) and neurological symptoms
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: The classic triad is severe back pain + systemic sepsis (fever/rigors) + neurological symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: New or changing lower-limb neurological signs in a patient with discitis most concerning for which complication?
options: An epidural abscess causing cord/nerve compression
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: An epidural abscess causing cord/nerve compression
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: New/changing lower-limb neurology suggests an epidural abscess compressing the cord or roots — a surgical emergency.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Why should blood cultures and biopsy ideally be obtained BEFORE starting antibiotics in discitis?
options: So treatment can be organism-directed once the pathogen is identified
Because cultures are only positive after antibiotics
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: So treatment can be organism-directed once the pathogen is identified
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Obtaining cultures/biopsy before antibiotics (where safe) identifies the organism, allowing organism-directed therapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the typical antibiotic treatment for discitis?
options: A single dose of oral antibiotics
A prolonged (6–8 week) IV course covering Staph aureus (e.g. flucloxacillin)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A prolonged (6–8 week) IV course covering Staph aureus (e.g. flucloxacillin)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Discitis requires a prolonged (typically 6–8 week) IV antibiotic course covering Staphylococcus aureus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for discitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: IV drug use
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: IV drug use, immunosuppression, diabetes, recent bacteraemia, spinal instrumentation and indwelling lines are risk factors for discitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: When is surgery indicated in discitis?
options: Only if antibiotics fail after 6 months
For an epidural abscess, cord compression or spinal instability
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: For an epidural abscess, cord compression or spinal instability
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Surgical drainage/decompression is indicated for an epidural abscess, cord compression or spinal instability (emergency with a neurological deficit).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A febrile patient with severe back pain is found to have discitis. Which combination of investigations is most appropriate?
options: MRI, blood cultures, CT-guided biopsy and echocardiography
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: MRI, blood cultures, CT-guided biopsy and echocardiography
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: The appropriate work-up is MRI (most sensitive), blood cultures, CT-guided biopsy (organism) and echocardiography (to exclude endocarditis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: How does the pain of discitis typically differ from mechanical back pain?
options: It eases with rest and is worse on movement
It is severe, unremitting and often present at night, with systemic sepsis
It is only present when walking uphill
It is relieved by bending forward
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: It is severe, unremitting and often present at night, with systemic sepsis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Discitis causes severe, unremitting night pain with systemic sepsis, unlike movement-related mechanical pain that eases with rest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Discitis with adjacent vertebral involvement is also known as:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Spondylodiscitis (vertebral osteomyelitis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Discitis with adjacent vertebral osteomyelitis is termed spondylodiscitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with diabetes and a recent line-related bacteraemia develops severe back pain and fever. Which diagnosis should be prioritised?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Discitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Recent bacteraemia and diabetes are risk factors; severe back pain with fever should prompt urgent assessment for discitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What supportive/source-control measures are part of discitis management?
options: ABCDE/sepsis six, treating endocarditis or the primary source, supportive care and spinal bracing as needed
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: ABCDE/sepsis six, treating endocarditis or the primary source, supportive care and spinal bracing as needed
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Alongside antibiotics/surgery, management includes ABCDE/sepsis six, treating the source (e.g. endocarditis), supportive care and spinal bracing as needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which statement about the origin of discitis is correct?
options: It is almost always from direct trauma
It never spreads to the epidural space
It is not associated with endocarditis
It is usually haematogenous, so a distant primary source must be sought
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: It is usually haematogenous, so a distant primary source must be sought
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Discitis is usually haematogenous, so the primary source (especially infective endocarditis) must be identified and treated.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A 78-year-old woman develops sudden mid-back pain after bending to lift a kettle. X-ray shows anterior wedging of a thoracic vertebra. She has lost 4 cm of height over recent years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Osteoporotic vertebral (fragility) fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Sudden back pain after minimal load, an anterior wedge fracture and height loss in an older woman is a classic osteoporotic vertebral fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which imaging modality best differentiates an osteoporotic vertebral fracture from a pathological (e.g. malignant) one?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: MRI
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: MRI differentiates a benign osteoporotic fracture (benign marrow pattern) from a pathological one (tumour/infection features).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: What is the classic X-ray appearance of an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
options: Anterior wedging (compression) of the vertebral body
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Anterior wedging (compression) of the vertebral body
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures classically show anterior wedging (compression) of the vertebral body on X-ray.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which is the KEY step after diagnosing an osteoporotic vertebral fracture, to prevent the next fracture?
options: Treating the underlying osteoporosis (calcium + vitamin D + a bisphosphonate)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Treating the underlying osteoporosis (calcium + vitamin D + a bisphosphonate)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: A fragility fracture is a strong indication to treat the underlying osteoporosis (calcium/vitamin D + bisphosphonate) to prevent recurrence.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which examination finding results from multiple thoracic osteoporotic wedge fractures?
options: A thoracic kyphosis ('dowager's hump') with height loss
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A thoracic kyphosis ('dowager's hump') with height loss
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Multiple thoracic wedge fractures produce a thoracic kyphosis ('dowager's hump') with progressive height loss.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which of the following is a red flag suggesting a pathological rather than osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
options: A history of previous cancer with night pain and systemic symptoms
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: A history of previous cancer with night pain and systemic symptoms
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Red flags such as previous cancer, night pain, systemic symptoms and neurology point to a pathological (malignant/infective) fracture and warrant MRI.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Prolonged glucocorticoid use
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Prolonged glucocorticoid use — along with age, low BMI, previous fragility fracture, smoking/alcohol and falls — is a risk factor for osteoporotic vertebral fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: How should the acute pain of a stable osteoporotic vertebral fracture be managed?
options: Adequate analgesia with early mobilisation and physiotherapy
Strict bed rest for several weeks
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Adequate analgesia with early mobilisation and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Stable fractures are managed with analgesia and early mobilisation (avoiding prolonged bed rest) plus physiotherapy; most heal conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: When is vertebroplasty or kyphoplasty considered for an osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
options: Only if there is cord compression
For severe, persistent pain not responding to conservative treatment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: For severe, persistent pain not responding to conservative treatment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty (cement injection) is considered for severe, persistent pain unresponsive to conservative management.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A fragility fracture in a patient over 50 allows the clinician to do what regarding osteoporosis assessment?
options: Arrange a DEXA scan without first performing a fracture-risk calculation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Arrange a DEXA scan without first performing a fracture-risk calculation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: A fragility fracture over age 50 is a strong enough indication to arrange DEXA directly, without needing a preceding risk-tool calculation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which osteoporotic vertebral fracture feature makes many of them easy to miss?
options: Many are asymptomatic and found incidentally
They only occur after major trauma
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Many are asymptomatic and found incidentally
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Many osteoporotic vertebral fractures are silent/asymptomatic and found incidentally, with height loss and kyphosis sometimes the only sign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Which investigations best combine to characterise the fracture AND assess the bone disease?
options: X-ray/CT/MRI for the fracture, plus DEXA/FRAX for the osteoporosis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: X-ray/CT/MRI for the fracture, plus DEXA/FRAX for the osteoporosis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: X-ray (wedge), CT (detail), MRI (exclude tumour) characterise the fracture, while DEXA/FRAX assess the underlying osteoporosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: A patient with a vertebral fracture develops new lower-limb weakness and urinary symptoms. What must be excluded urgently?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: Cord or cauda equina compression
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: New neurological symptoms with a vertebral fracture require urgent exclusion of cord/cauda equina compression.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: Why is prolonged bed rest avoided in osteoporotic vertebral fracture?
options: It causes deconditioning and further bone loss
It prevents healing of the wedge
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: It causes deconditioning and further bone loss
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Prolonged bed rest leads to deconditioning and further bone loss, so early mobilisation is preferred.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.question: At which region of the spine do osteoporotic vertebral fractures most typically occur?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.answer: The thoracolumbar junction
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Lower Back & S.explanation: Osteoporotic vertebral fractures most typically occur at the thoracolumbar junction; fractures of the posterior elements should raise suspicion of malignancy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: A 28-year-old marathon runner develops sharp lateral knee pain that comes on after a predictable distance and eases with rest. Tenderness is maximal about 2–3 cm above the lateral joint line. There is no effusion or locking. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Lateral knee pain in a runner with point tenderness 2–3 cm above the joint line and no effusion/locking is classic iliotibial band syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Against which bony structure does the iliotibial band rub to cause ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Repeated knee flexion/extension makes the ITB rub against the lateral femoral epicondyle, causing friction and pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Where does the iliotibial band insert distally?
options: Gerdy's tubercle (just below the lateral knee)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Gerdy's tubercle (just below the lateral knee)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: The ITB inserts onto Gerdy's tubercle, just below the lateral aspect of the knee.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Which biomechanical factor is a key risk factor for ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Weak hip abductors (gluteus medius) are a key biomechanical risk factor, along with genu varum, tight ITB and training errors.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: At approximately what knee flexion angle is the pain of ITBS typically worst?
options: It is unrelated to knee angle
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: ITBS pain is characteristically worst around 30° of knee flexion, where friction over the lateral epicondyle is greatest.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Which feature best distinguishes ITBS from a lateral meniscal tear?
options: ITBS causes joint-line pain with locking
A meniscal tear is worse downhill running
ITBS causes tenderness ABOVE the joint line from overuse, whereas a meniscal tear causes joint-LINE pain with locking after a twist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: ITBS causes tenderness ABOVE the joint line from overuse, whereas a meniscal tear causes joint-LINE pain with locking after a twist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: ITBS gives tenderness 2–3 cm above the joint line from overuse; a meniscal tear gives joint-line pain with locking/catching after a twisting injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Which activity most characteristically worsens ITBS pain?
options: Running, especially downhill or on stairs
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Running, especially downhill or on stairs
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: ITBS pain is worse with running, particularly downhill or on stairs, and comes on after a predictable distance.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: How is ITBS diagnosed?
options: MRI of the knee in all cases
Clinically — from the runner history and characteristic lateral tenderness (± Noble's test)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Clinically — from the runner history and characteristic lateral tenderness (± Noble's test)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: ITBS is a clinical diagnosis based on the history and lateral epicondyle tenderness, with Noble's test supporting it; imaging is reserved for unclear/refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: What is Noble's test used to assess?
options: ITBS — pressure over the lateral femoral epicondyle while extending the flexed knee reproduces pain
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: ITBS — pressure over the lateral femoral epicondyle while extending the flexed knee reproduces pain
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Noble's test reproduces ITBS pain by pressing over the lateral femoral epicondyle as the flexed knee is extended.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: What is the KEY active treatment for ITBS?
options: Physiotherapy — ITB/hip stretching plus hip-abductor (gluteus medius) strengthening
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Physiotherapy — ITB/hip stretching plus hip-abductor (gluteus medius) strengthening
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Physiotherapy with stretching and hip-abductor strengthening (plus biomechanical/technique correction) is the key active treatment for ITBS.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: What is the appropriate first-line management for a runner with ITBS?
options: Activity modification (reduce mileage, avoid downhill), analgesia and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Activity modification (reduce mileage, avoid downhill), analgesia and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: First-line management is conservative — relative rest/activity modification, NSAIDs/ice and physiotherapy; most cases resolve conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: A patient with anterior knee pain around and behind the kneecap, worse on stairs and prolonged sitting, most likely has which condition rather than ITBS?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Anterior/peripatellar pain worse on stairs and prolonged sitting is patellofemoral pain syndrome, whereas ITBS is lateral with tenderness above the joint line.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Which of the following is a recognised training-related risk factor for ITBS?
options: A sudden increase in running mileage and downhill running
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: A sudden increase in running mileage and downhill running
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Sudden mileage increases, downhill running and cambered surfaces are training-related risk factors for ITBS.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: What is the role of corticosteroid injection and surgery in ITBS?
options: Reserved for refractory cases — occasional injection to the point of friction, with ITB release/lengthening a rare last resort
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: Reserved for refractory cases — occasional injection to the point of friction, with ITB release/lengthening a rare last resort
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: Injection and surgery (ITB release/lengthening) are reserved for refractory ITBS after conservative management fails.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.question: Which examination finding argues AGAINST an intra-articular cause and supports ITBS?
options: No effusion and no locking/catching, with tenderness above the joint line
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.answer: No effusion and no locking/catching, with tenderness above the joint line
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Iliotibial Ban.explanation: The absence of effusion and locking, with tenderness above the joint line, points away from intra-articular pathology and towards ITBS.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A new mother presents with pain on the radial side of her wrist, worse when lifting her baby. She is tender over the radial styloid, and pain is reproduced when she tucks her thumb into a fist and the wrist is deviated towards the ulnar side. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: De Quervain's tenosynovitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Radial styloid tenderness with a positive Finkelstein's test in someone with repetitive thumb use (a new mother) is classic De Quervain's tenosynovitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which two tendons are affected in De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)
Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Flexor pollicis longus and flexor carpi radialis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Abductor pollicis longus (APL) and extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: De Quervain's affects the APL and EPB tendons in the first dorsal (extensor) compartment at the radial wrist.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Through which compartment do the affected tendons run in De Quervain's?
options: The first dorsal (extensor) compartment, under the extensor retinaculum
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The first dorsal (extensor) compartment, under the extensor retinaculum
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The APL and EPB pass through the first dorsal (extensor) compartment beneath the extensor retinaculum at the radial wrist.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: How is Finkelstein's test performed?
options: Percussing over the median nerve at the wrist
Axial loading of the thumb (grind test)
Making a fist with the thumb tucked inside the fingers, then ulnar-deviating the wrist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Making a fist with the thumb tucked inside the fingers, then ulnar-deviating the wrist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Finkelstein's test tucks the thumb into a fist and ulnar-deviates the wrist, straining the APL/EPB tendons — radial wrist pain is a positive result.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Where is the characteristic point of tenderness in De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: The A1 pulley of the palm
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The radial styloid
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The radial styloid (over the first extensor compartment) is the characteristic tender spot in De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: An older patient has pain and squaring at the base of the thumb with a positive grind test. Which diagnosis is this, rather than De Quervain's?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Thumb-base (CMC) osteoarthritis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Pain and squaring at the CMC joint with a positive grind test in an older patient indicates thumb-base (CMC) osteoarthritis, not De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A young man presents with radial wrist pain after falling onto an outstretched hand, with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox. What must be excluded?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A scaphoid fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness after a FOOSH indicates a possible scaphoid fracture, which must be excluded — distinct from the radial styloid tenderness of De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: How is De Quervain's tenosynovitis diagnosed?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Clinically, confirmed by Finkelstein's test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: De Quervain's is a clinical diagnosis confirmed by Finkelstein's test; imaging (ultrasound) is used only if the diagnosis is unclear.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the first-line management of De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: A thumb spica splint with activity modification and analgesia
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A thumb spica splint with activity modification and analgesia
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: First-line management is conservative: a thumb spica splint, activity modification and analgesia/NSAIDs.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which intervention is often highly effective for De Quervain's when conservative measures fail?
options: Corticosteroid injection into the first extensor compartment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Corticosteroid injection into the first extensor compartment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A corticosteroid injection into the first extensor compartment is often highly effective in De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the surgical option for refractory De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: Release of the extensor retinaculum (first compartment)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Release of the extensor retinaculum (first compartment)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Surgical release of the extensor retinaculum over the first compartment relieves pressure and makes space for the tendons in resistant cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which underlying process best describes De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: A stenosing tenosynovitis with impaired tendon gliding through a tight compartment
A bacterial infection of the tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A stenosing tenosynovitis with impaired tendon gliding through a tight compartment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: De Quervain's is a stenosing tenosynovitis — inflammation/swelling thickens the sheath in the tight first compartment, impairing tendon gliding.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient reports fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers with palpable thickening of the palmar fascia, and has a history of alcohol use. Which hand disorder is this?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Dupuytren's contracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Palmar fascia fibrosis causing fixed flexion of the ring/little fingers, linked with alcohol/diabetes/family history, is Dupuytren's contracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient's finger clicks and intermittently locks in a flexed position, with a tender nodule felt at the base of the finger in the palm. Which diagnosis fits?
options: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis at the A1 pulley)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A flexor tendon nodule catching at the A1 pulley, causing clicking/locking in flexion, is trigger finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A firm, well-defined swelling on the dorsal wrist transilluminates on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Ganglion cyst
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A mucin-filled cyst from a joint/tendon sheath that transilluminates, commonly on the dorsal wrist, is a ganglion cyst (which often resolves spontaneously).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which occupational/behavioural pattern is most associated with De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
options: Repetitive thumb and wrist use (e.g. lifting a baby, texting)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Repetitive thumb and wrist use (e.g. lifting a baby, texting)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Repetitive thumb/wrist movements — lifting babies, texting/typing, occupational tasks — precipitate De Quervain's ('mother's/gamer's thumb').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which examination finding, besides radial styloid tenderness, supports De Quervain's tenosynovitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Painful resisted thumb abduction
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Painful resisted thumb abduction (worse with gripping/lifting/wringing), along with radial styloid tenderness and positive Finkelstein's, supports De Quervain's.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A lactating woman with De Quervain's asks about prognosis. What is the best advice?
options: It is permanent and needs early surgery
Pregnancy/lactation-related cases often resolve once the precipitant settles, alongside conservative measures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Pregnancy/lactation-related cases often resolve once the precipitant settles, alongside conservative measures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Pregnancy/lactation-related De Quervain's often improves once the precipitant (e.g. baby-lifting) settles, managed conservatively in the meantime.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A 62-year-old man of Northern European descent with a history of alcohol excess notices his right ring finger is gradually curling into the palm and cannot be fully straightened. There is a firm cord in the palm but no pain. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Dupuytren's contracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A painless, progressive fixed flexion of the ring finger with a palpable palmar cord, in a patient with typical risk factors, is Dupuytren's contracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which structure undergoes progressive fibrosis in Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The palmar (palmar aponeurosis) fascia
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's is a progressive fibrosis of the palmar fascia, forming nodules and cords that flex the fingers.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which finger is MOST commonly affected in Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The ring finger
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The ring finger (± little finger) is most commonly affected; the index finger is least likely to be involved.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which drug is the classic cause of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Phenytoin
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Phenytoin is the classic drug cause of Dupuytren's contracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the FIRST sign of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Hard nodules on the palm
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Hard palmar nodules (with skin thickening/pitting) are the first sign, before cords and contracture develop.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the inheritance pattern of Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Autosomal dominant
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's is strongly hereditary with an autosomal dominant pattern.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: How is Dupuytren's contracture diagnosed?
options: Clinically — a palpable cord/nodule and the table-top test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Clinically — a palpable cord/nodule and the table-top test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's is a clinical diagnosis based on a palpable cord/nodule and the table-top test; no imaging is needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient with Dupuytren's cannot lay the affected hand flat on a table. What does this positive table-top test indicate?
options: A significant contracture — a marker for surgical referral
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A significant contracture — a marker for surgical referral
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A positive table-top test (inability to rest the hand flat) indicates a significant contracture and prompts surgical referral.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: When is surgery indicated in Dupuytren's contracture?
options: When the MCP joints cannot be straightened and the hand cannot lie flat (positive table-top test)
As soon as a nodule appears
Only if the finger is painful
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: When the MCP joints cannot be straightened and the hand cannot lie flat (positive table-top test)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Surgery is triggered by the functional threshold: MCP joints that cannot be straightened and a positive table-top test.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which is the LEAST invasive surgical option for Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Needle fasciotomy (aponeurotomy)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Needle fasciotomy, in which a needle divides/loosens the cord, is the least invasive surgical option.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which is the MOST extensive surgical procedure for severe/recurrent Dupuytren's contracture?
options: Dermofasciectomy (fascia + cord + overlying skin with a graft)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Dermofasciectomy (fascia + cord + overlying skin with a graft)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dermofasciectomy removes the fascia, cord and overlying skin with a skin graft — the most extensive option, for recurrent/severe disease.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which feature best distinguishes Dupuytren's contracture from trigger finger?
options: Dupuytren's causes painful catching and locking
Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with no catching or snapping
Dupuytren's affects the tendon sheath at the A1 pulley
Dupuytren's is confirmed by Finkelstein's test
Dupuytren's mainly affects the index finger
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with no catching or snapping
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion without catching/snapping, whereas trigger finger causes painful catching/clicking/locking at the A1 pulley.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A non-surgical enzymatic option that can dissolve the Dupuytren's cord is:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Collagenase injection
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Collagenase injection enzymatically dissolves the cord and is a non-surgical alternative in some settings.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which of the following is a recognised risk factor for Dupuytren's contracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Alcoholic liver disease
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Alcoholic liver disease/alcohol excess, diabetes, family history, phenytoin, vibrating-tool manual labour and hand trauma are recognised risk factors.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the typical natural history of Dupuytren's contracture after surgical treatment?
options: It resolves spontaneously in all cases
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It tends to recur
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's contracture tends to recur after treatment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient has painless palmar nodules with skin puckering and early curling of the little finger. Which associated conditions should be screened for?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Diabetes and alcohol/liver disease
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Dupuytren's is associated with diabetes and alcohol/liver disease, which can be screened for given the clinical presentation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A 55-year-old woman with diabetes notices her right middle finger catches and locks in a bent position each morning, then suddenly snaps straight with a painful click. A tender nodule is felt at the base of the finger on the palm. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Trigger finger
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A finger that catches/locks in flexion and snaps straight with a click, plus a palm-side MCP nodule, is trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: At which pulley does the flexor tendon most commonly catch in trigger finger?
options: The A1 pulley at the MCP joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The A1 pulley at the MCP joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger most commonly involves the first annular (A1) pulley at the MCP joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the mechanical basis of trigger finger?
options: A size mismatch between a thickened flexor tendon (± nodule) and the tight A1 pulley
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A size mismatch between a thickened flexor tendon (± nodule) and the tight A1 pulley
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger is a mechanical size mismatch — a swollen tendon/nodule cannot glide smoothly through the unyielding A1 pulley.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which digits are most commonly affected by trigger finger?
options: The thumb, middle or ring finger
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The thumb, middle or ring finger
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The thumb, middle and ring fingers are most commonly affected in trigger finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: When are the symptoms of trigger finger typically worst?
options: Only at night with no daytime symptoms
In the morning, improving through the day
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: In the morning, improving through the day
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger symptoms are typically worse in the morning and improve during the day.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which is a recognised risk factor for trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Diabetes mellitus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger is idiopathic in most, but associations include female sex, rheumatoid arthritis and diabetes mellitus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: How is trigger finger diagnosed?
options: Clinically — the triggering plus a palpable nodule
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Clinically — the triggering plus a palpable nodule
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger is a clinical diagnosis based on the catching/locking and a palpable nodule; no imaging is needed.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the FIRST-line treatment for trigger finger?
options: A corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath at the A1 pulley
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath at the A1 pulley
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A corticosteroid injection into the flexor tendon sheath at the A1 pulley is first-line and is successful in most patients.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the surgical procedure for trigger finger that fails conservative treatment?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A1 pulley release
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A1 pulley release (dividing the A1 pulley to free the tendon) is the surgical option when steroid injection fails.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which feature best distinguishes trigger finger from Dupuytren's contracture?
options: Trigger finger is painless fixed flexion
Trigger finger has a palmar cord
Dupuytren's causes locking that snaps straight
Both are confirmed by Finkelstein's test
Trigger finger causes painful catching/snapping and a nodule, whereas Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with a cord and no snapping
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Trigger finger causes painful catching/snapping and a nodule, whereas Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with a cord and no snapping
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Trigger finger is painful with catching/snapping at the A1 pulley; Dupuytren's is painless fixed flexion with a palmar cord and no locking/snapping.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Describe what happens to the tendon nodule during extension in trigger finger.
options: It slides freely through the pulley
It gets stuck at the entrance to the A1 pulley, so the finger locks in flexion then releases with a snap
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It gets stuck at the entrance to the A1 pulley, so the finger locks in flexion then releases with a snap
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: On extension the nodule catches at the entrance to the A1 pulley, locking the finger in flexion until it releases suddenly with a painful pop — the 'trigger'.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient has painless, gradual fixed flexion of the ring finger with a palpable palmar cord and no catching or snapping. Which diagnosis is this, rather than trigger finger?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Dupuytren's contracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Painless fixed flexion with a palmar cord and no snapping is Dupuytren's contracture, not trigger finger.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the role of a splint in trigger finger?
options: To hold the finger in extension (especially at night) alongside activity modification
To immobilise the wrist for 6 weeks
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: To hold the finger in extension (especially at night) alongside activity modification
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A finger splint holding the digit in extension (particularly at night), with activity modification and NSAIDs, is used as part of conservative management.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Where would you palpate for the characteristic nodule in trigger finger?
options: At the base of the affected finger on the palm side (over the MCP/A1 pulley)
The ulnar border of the hand
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: At the base of the affected finger on the palm side (over the MCP/A1 pulley)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The nodule is felt on the palm side at the base of the affected finger, over the MCP joint/A1 pulley.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops a finger that intermittently locks in flexion. Which condition should be considered?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Trigger finger (stenosing tenosynovitis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis is a recognised association of trigger finger, which causes intermittent locking of the finger in flexion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A 30-year-old presents with a firm, well-circumscribed, painless lump on the dorsum of the wrist that fluctuates in size. It transilluminates when a light is shone through it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: A giant cell tumour of the tendon sheath
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A ganglion cyst
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A firm, well-circumscribed, painless swelling on the dorsal wrist that transilluminates is a ganglion cyst — the commonest hand/wrist lump.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which clinical sign helps confirm that a wrist lump is a ganglion cyst rather than a solid tumour?
options: It transilluminates when light is shone through it
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It transilluminates when light is shone through it
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A ganglion is fluid-filled, so it transilluminates; solid lumps do not.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: From what does a ganglion cyst arise?
options: A joint capsule or tendon sheath (via a stalk)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A joint capsule or tendon sheath (via a stalk)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A ganglion is a synovial cyst that balloons out from a joint capsule or tendon sheath through a stalk, filled with jelly-like synovial fluid.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Where is the commonest site for a ganglion cyst?
options: The palm over the A1 pulley
The dorsal aspect of the wrist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: The dorsal aspect of the wrist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: The dorsal wrist is the commonest site for a ganglion cyst.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the first-line management of a typical, asymptomatic ganglion cyst?
options: Reassurance and observation, as many resolve spontaneously
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Reassurance and observation, as many resolve spontaneously
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Most ganglia are harmless and many resolve spontaneously, so first-line management is reassurance and observation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A patient requests treatment for a symptomatic ganglion. Which statement about aspiration is correct?
options: It is curative with no recurrence
It is simple but has a high recurrence rate
It is contraindicated in all ganglia
It always requires a general anaesthetic
