It converts the cyst into a solid tumour
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It is simple but has a high recurrence rate
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Aspiration (± steroid) is simple but carries a high recurrence rate.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: When is surgical excision indicated for a ganglion cyst?
options: For any ganglion on first presentation
For severe/persistent symptoms or neurovascular compromise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: For severe/persistent symptoms or neurovascular compromise
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Surgical excision (of the cyst and its stalk) is reserved for severe/persistent symptoms or neurovascular compromise; it has lower recurrence than aspiration but can still recur.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A finger lump at the DIP joint associated with osteoarthritis is best described as:
options: A mucous cyst (a type of ganglion)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: A mucous cyst (a type of ganglion)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A ganglion at the DIP joint in osteoarthritis is called a mucous cyst.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which feature would make a wrist lump CONCERNING and warrant imaging to exclude another lesion?
options: It is painless and near a tendon sheath
It is solid, non-transilluminating, fixed and rapidly growing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It is solid, non-transilluminating, fixed and rapidly growing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A solid, non-transilluminating, fixed, rapidly growing or painful lump is concerning and warrants imaging to exclude another lesion.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: How is a ganglion cyst usually diagnosed?
options: Clinically, using the site and a firm, transilluminating, well-circumscribed swelling
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Clinically, using the site and a firm, transilluminating, well-circumscribed swelling
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A ganglion is a clinical diagnosis (site + transillumination); imaging is reserved for atypical cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: Which investigation is most appropriate if the diagnosis of a ganglion is uncertain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Ultrasound
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Ultrasound is used if uncertain — it confirms a cyst, assesses its connection and any solid component; MRI is rarely needed for atypical/deep lesions.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the nature of the fluid within a ganglion cyst?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Thick, jelly-like synovial fluid
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: A ganglion contains thick, jelly-like synovial fluid, having ballooned from a joint capsule or tendon sheath.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What advice should be given about the old 'Bible therapy' (hitting the cyst with a heavy book)?
options: It should not be done — it is ineffective and harmful
It is an effective first-line treatment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It should not be done — it is ineffective and harmful
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: 'Bible therapy' (striking the cyst with a heavy book) is an old myth that is ineffective and harmful and should not be done.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: A ganglion is pressing on a nearby nerve, causing paraesthesia. What is the appropriate management?
options: Consider intervention (aspiration or surgical excision) because of the neurovascular symptoms
Ignore it as it is benign
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: Consider intervention (aspiration or surgical excision) because of the neurovascular symptoms
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Neurovascular compromise (e.g. nerve compression causing paraesthesia) is an indication to intervene with aspiration or surgical excision, despite the ganglion being benign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.question: What is the typical natural history of a ganglion cyst?
options: It is benign and many resolve spontaneously
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.answer: It is benign and many resolve spontaneously
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Hand & Wrist D.explanation: Ganglia are completely benign, and many resolve spontaneously after a few months.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A 40-year-old recreational footballer feels a sudden pain 'like being kicked in the back of the leg' and hears a pop while pushing off. He can weakly move the foot downwards. Which test best confirms the likely diagnosis?
options: Asking him to plantarflex against resistance
The anterior drawer test of the ankle
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: The calf-squeeze (Simmonds'/Thompson's) test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A ruptured Achilles can still weakly plantarflex via other muscles, so the calf-squeeze test is decisive — no plantarflexion on squeezing the calf indicates rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which is the commonest cause of posterior heel pain?
options: Gout of the first MTP joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Achilles tendon disorders
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Achilles tendon disorders (a spectrum from tendinopathy to rupture) are the commonest cause of posterior heel pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which class of antibiotic is a classic cause of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Fluoroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin are a well-recognised (MHRA-warned) cause of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture — stop the quinolone if tendon pain develops.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A 55-year-old runner has gradual-onset posterior heel pain, worse after running, with morning stiffness and a tender, thickened tendon. The calf-squeeze produces normal plantarflexion. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Achilles tendinopathy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Gradual heel pain worse after activity with morning stiffness and an intact calf-squeeze is Achilles tendinopathy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is the KEY active treatment for Achilles tendinopathy?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Eccentric calf-strengthening exercises
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Eccentric calf-strengthening exercises are the key active treatment; corticosteroid injection is avoided as it increases rupture risk.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Why should corticosteroid injection be avoided in Achilles tendinopathy?
options: It increases the risk of tendon rupture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: It increases the risk of tendon rupture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Local corticosteroid injection weakens the tendon and increases the risk of Achilles rupture, so it is avoided.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: On the calf-squeeze (Simmonds') test, what finding indicates a complete Achilles rupture?
options: No plantarflexion — the foot stays neutral
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: No plantarflexion — the foot stays neutral
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: In a complete rupture, squeezing the calf produces no plantarflexion (the foot stays neutral) — a positive Simmonds'/Thompson's test.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which is the first-line investigation to confirm a suspected Achilles tendon rupture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Ultrasound
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Ultrasound is the first-line imaging to confirm an Achilles rupture and demonstrate the gap.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: In the conservative management of an Achilles rupture, in which position is the ankle immobilised?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantarflexion (equinus)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The ankle is immobilised in plantarflexion (equinus) to approximate the torn tendon ends and allow healing.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient with a suspected Achilles rupture asks why the doctor is not reassured that he can still move his foot down. What is the best explanation?
options: Other muscles (tibialis posterior, toe flexors, peroneals) can still weakly plantarflex, so this does not exclude rupture
Plantarflexion is impossible with a ruptured Achilles
He must have only a sprain
The Achilles does not plantarflex the foot
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Other muscles (tibialis posterior, toe flexors, peroneals) can still weakly plantarflex, so this does not exclude rupture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A ruptured Achilles can still weakly plantarflex using other muscles, so preserved plantarflexion does not exclude rupture — hence the calf-squeeze test.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Besides fluoroquinolones, which metabolic condition predisposes to both Achilles tendinopathy and rupture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Hypercholesterolaemia
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Hypercholesterolaemia predisposes to Achilles disorders through lipid deposition in the tendon (xanthomata).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which position and manoeuvre are used to elicit the classic signs of an Achilles rupture?
options: Prone with the feet over the edge of the bed, observing declination, palpating for a gap and squeezing the calf
Supine with the knee flexed, testing dorsiflexion
Lying on the side with the hip flexed
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Prone with the feet over the edge of the bed, observing declination, palpating for a gap and squeezing the calf
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The patient lies prone with feet over the bed edge; you observe the angle of declination, palpate for a gap and perform the calf-squeeze — Simmonds' triad.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: When is surgical repair (rather than conservative management) typically favoured for an Achilles rupture?
options: In younger patients/athletes, delayed presentation, or re-rupture
Whenever the patient can weakly plantarflex
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: In younger patients/athletes, delayed presentation, or re-rupture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Surgical repair is favoured for selected patients — younger patients/athletes, delayed presentation or re-rupture — while many are managed conservatively in an equinus boot.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient on ciprofloxacin for a UTI develops new Achilles pain. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Start eccentric exercises immediately while continuing the drug
Stop the quinolone and assess the tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Stop the quinolone and assess the tendon
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Quinolone-associated tendon pain warrants stopping the quinolone (per MHRA advice) and assessing for tendinopathy/rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which examination finding is characteristic of Achilles tendinopathy (as opposed to rupture)?
options: A palpable gap in the tendon
A tender, thickened but intact tendon with preserved calf-squeeze
Greater dorsiflexion of the resting foot
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: A tender, thickened but intact tendon with preserved calf-squeeze
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Tendinopathy gives a tender, thickened but intact tendon with a normal (preserved) calf-squeeze, unlike the gap and lost calf-squeeze of rupture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What should be done for a patient with a clinically suspected Achilles rupture while awaiting orthopaedic review?
options: Encourage full weight-bearing and normal walking
Apply the ankle in full dorsiflexion
Keep the limb immobilised in equinus/non-weight-bearing
Discharge with simple analgesia and no follow-up
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Keep the limb immobilised in equinus/non-weight-bearing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Keep the ankle immobilised in plantarflexion (equinus) and non-weight-bearing until orthopaedic review, to protect the approximated tendon ends.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: The Ottawa ankle rules are used to determine which injured ankles require:
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: An X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The Ottawa ankle rules identify which ankle injuries need an X-ray, reducing unnecessary imaging.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient presents with inferior heel pain that is worst on the first few steps in the morning and eases with walking. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantar fasciitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Inferior heel pain worst on the first steps is characteristic of plantar fasciitis (in contrast to the posterior heel pain of Achilles disorders).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A footballer rolls their ankle inward (inversion) and has swelling and tenderness just anterior and inferior to the lateral malleolus, but can weight-bear. Which ligament is most likely injured?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: The anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: An inversion injury with tenderness anterior/inferior to the lateral malleolus is a low sprain, most commonly of the ATFL — the weakest and most commonly injured lateral ligament.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which mechanism characteristically causes a HIGH (syndesmotic) ankle sprain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: External rotation of the foot
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A high (syndesmotic) sprain results from external rotation, where the talus pushes the fibula laterally and strains the syndesmosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which bedside test suggests a syndesmotic (high) ankle sprain?
options: The Hopkins squeeze test (squeezing tibia and fibula at mid-calf reproduces pain)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: The Hopkins squeeze test (squeezing tibia and fibula at mid-calf reproduces pain)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A positive Hopkins squeeze test — pain when the tibia and fibula are squeezed together at mid-calf — indicates a syndesmotic (high) sprain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: According to the Ottawa ankle rules, an ankle X-ray is indicated if there is malleolar-zone pain AND one of which findings?
options: Inability to weight-bear for 4 steps, OR bony tenderness at the distal tibia or distal fibula
Pain lasting more than a week
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Inability to weight-bear for 4 steps, OR bony tenderness at the distal tibia or distal fibula
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The Ottawa ankle rules require malleolar-zone pain plus inability to weight-bear 4 steps or bony tenderness at the posterior edge/tip of the medial or lateral malleolus.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is the main purpose of the Ottawa ankle rules?
options: To grade the severity of a sprain
To minimise unnecessary X-rays while reliably detecting significant fractures
To classify fractures by Weber type
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: To minimise unnecessary X-rays while reliably detecting significant fractures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The Ottawa ankle rules are highly sensitive for clinically significant fractures, allowing unnecessary X-rays to be safely avoided.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A high ankle sprain is confirmed and the X-ray shows widening of the tibiofibular joint. What does this finding indicate for management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Diastasis — operative fixation is indicated
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Tibiofibular widening (diastasis) indicates an unstable syndesmotic injury requiring operative fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What proportion of ankle sprains are 'low' (lateral collateral) sprains?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: More than 90%
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Low (lateral collateral) sprains account for more than 90% of ankle sprains and are usually benign.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A grade III low ankle sprain is characterised by:
options: A microscopic stretch with mild pain and full weight-bearing
A partial tear with moderate swelling only
A complete ligament tear with severe pain, marked instability and difficulty weight-bearing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: A complete ligament tear with severe pain, marked instability and difficulty weight-bearing
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A grade III sprain is a complete ligament tear with severe pain/swelling, marked instability and difficulty weight-bearing (grade I = stretch, grade II = partial tear).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which set of structures constitutes the ankle syndesmosis?
options: AITFL, PITFL, the interosseous ligament and interosseous membrane
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: AITFL, PITFL, the interosseous ligament and interosseous membrane
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The syndesmosis comprises the AITFL, PITFL, interosseous ligament and interosseous membrane, binding the distal tibia and fibula.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is the first-line management of a low (lateral) ankle sprain?
options: Conservative management — RICE, then early mobilisation and rehab
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Conservative management — RICE, then early mobilisation and rehab
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Low ankle sprains are managed conservatively with RICE, short-term support, then early mobilisation and physiotherapy to prevent chronic instability.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: How is a HIGH ankle sprain WITHOUT diastasis managed?
options: RICE and immediate return to sport
A non-weight-bearing orthosis or cast until pain subsides
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: A non-weight-bearing orthosis or cast until pain subsides
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A stable syndesmotic sprain without diastasis is managed with a non-weight-bearing orthosis or cast until pain settles; diastasis or failed conservative treatment needs surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Why is proprioceptive and strengthening rehabilitation emphasised after a low ankle sprain?
options: To prevent chronic ankle instability and recurrent sprains
To avoid the need for an X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: To prevent chronic ankle instability and recurrent sprains
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Rehab with proprioception and strengthening reduces the risk of chronic instability and recurrent sprains after a lateral ankle sprain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient has a very painful, weight-bearing-limited ankle after an external rotation injury, with a positive squeeze test but a normal initial X-ray. What is the next best investigation?
options: Repeat the same X-ray in 6 weeks
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: MRI to assess the syndesmosis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: When a syndesmotic injury is strongly suspected but the X-ray is normal, MRI is used to assess the syndesmosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which ligament of the lateral complex is injured FIRST in an inversion ankle sprain?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The ATFL, the weakest lateral ligament, is injured first and most commonly in inversion sprains.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: How do ankle FRACTURES (as opposed to sprains) get classified, and how are they triaged from sprains?
options: By the Ottawa rules into grades I–III
By the Weber classification (A/B/C relative to the syndesmosis), with the Ottawa rules triaging sprain vs fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: By the Weber classification (A/B/C relative to the syndesmosis), with the Ottawa rules triaging sprain vs fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Ankle fractures are classified by the Weber system (A below, B at, C above the syndesmosis); the Ottawa ankle rules triage between sprain and fracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Compared with a low ankle sprain, a high (syndesmotic) sprain is:
options: More disabling, more painful on weight-bearing and slower to heal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: More disabling, more painful on weight-bearing and slower to heal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: High syndesmotic sprains are more disabling, more painful on weight-bearing and slower to heal than low sprains, and may need surgery if diastasis is present.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient meets none of the Ottawa ankle rule criteria after an inversion injury. What is the most appropriate management?
options: No X-ray needed; treat as a sprain with RICE and rehab
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: No X-ray needed; treat as a sprain with RICE and rehab
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A negative Ottawa rule assessment safely excludes clinically significant fracture, so no X-ray is needed and the sprain is managed conservatively.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Where should you palpate for bony tenderness of the distal fibula when applying the Ottawa ankle rules?
options: The base of the fifth metatarsal only
The posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: The posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: The Ottawa ankle rules assess bony tenderness over the posterior edge/tip of the lateral malleolus (distal fibula) and correspondingly the medial malleolus (distal tibia).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A 50-year-old shop worker describes sharp inferior heel pain that is worst with the first few steps out of bed each morning and eases as she walks around. Tenderness is maximal over the inner aspect of the heel. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantar fasciitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Inferior heel pain worst on the first morning steps, easing with activity, with tenderness over the medial calcaneal tuberosity, is classic plantar fasciitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Where is tenderness maximal in plantar fasciitis?
options: The lateral border of the foot
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: The medial calcaneal tuberosity (inferior heel)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Tenderness is maximal over the medial calcaneal tuberosity — the origin of the plantar fascia on the inferior/medial heel.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which is the commonest cause of heel pain in adults?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantar fasciitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Plantar fasciitis is the commonest cause of adult heel pain — a degenerative overuse condition of the plantar fascia origin.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which movement characteristically worsens plantar fasciitis pain by tensioning the fascia (the windlass mechanism)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Dorsiflexion of the toes
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Dorsiflexion of the toes tensions the plantar fascia via the windlass mechanism, reproducing/worsening the pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient's heel pain is actually located higher, at the posterior calcaneal insertion, rather than under the heel. Which diagnosis does this suggest instead of plantar fasciitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Achilles tendinopathy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Pain at the posterior calcaneal (Achilles) insertion suggests Achilles tendinopathy rather than the inferior heel pain of plantar fasciitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient with heel/foot pain has sensory loss along the lateral border of the foot, weak plantarflexion and an absent ankle jerk. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: S1 radiculopathy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Lateral foot sensory loss, weak plantarflexion and a lost ankle jerk indicate an S1 radiculopathy, not plantar fasciitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: How is plantar fasciitis diagnosed?
options: MRI of the foot in all cases
X-ray to demonstrate a heel spur
Clinically — from the history and tenderness over the medial calcaneal tuberosity
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Clinically — from the history and tenderness over the medial calcaneal tuberosity
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Plantar fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is reserved for atypical or refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A heel spur is seen on the X-ray of a patient with heel pain. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is the definite cause of the pain and needs excision
It confirms a calcaneal stress fracture
It is common and usually incidental — not the cause
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: It is common and usually incidental — not the cause
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A calcaneal (heel) spur is a common incidental finding and is not the cause of plantar fasciitis pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is the KEY active treatment for plantar fasciitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantar fascia and calf/Achilles stretching
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Plantar fascia and calf/Achilles stretching is the key active treatment, alongside supportive footwear and activity modification.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is the typical prognosis of plantar fasciitis?
options: Progressive and requires surgery in most
Self-limiting, with most resolving within ~6–12 months with conservative measures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Self-limiting, with most resolving within ~6–12 months with conservative measures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Plantar fasciitis is self-limiting — the majority resolve within about 6–12 months with conservative treatment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A young man presents with BILATERAL heel pain and a history of low back stiffness. Besides plantar fasciitis, what should be considered?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: A seronegative spondyloarthropathy (enthesitis)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Bilateral heel pain or plantar fasciitis in a young patient should prompt consideration of a seronegative spondyloarthropathy with enthesitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which is an appropriate conservative measure for plantar fasciitis?
options: Supportive footwear with insoles/heel pads and night splints
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Supportive footwear with insoles/heel pads and night splints
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Supportive footwear, insoles/heel pads and night splints (with stretching and activity modification) are first-line conservative measures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: What is a recognised risk of a corticosteroid injection for refractory plantar fasciitis?
options: Plantar fascia rupture and heel fat-pad atrophy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Plantar fascia rupture and heel fat-pad atrophy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Steroid injection gives short-term relief but carries a small risk of plantar fascia rupture and fat-pad atrophy, so it is used judiciously.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: A patient has forefoot pain with a palpable, tender thickening between the 3rd and 4th toes, worse when standing on tip-toes. Which diagnosis is this, not plantar fasciitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Morton's neuroma
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Forefoot pain with interdigital thickening between the 3rd and 4th toes, worse on tip-toes, is Morton's neuroma — a forefoot problem, not inferior heel pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: An athletic runner has heel pain reproduced by squeezing the sides of the calcaneus. Which diagnosis should be considered rather than plantar fasciitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Calcaneal stress fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Pain on squeezing the calcaneus suggests a calcaneal stress fracture (seen in athletes/osteoporosis), distinct from the focal fascial-origin tenderness of plantar fasciitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: Which risk factor is commonly associated with plantar fasciitis?
options: Prolonged standing, running, obesity and a tight calf/Achilles
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: Prolonged standing, running, obesity and a tight calf/Achilles
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: Mechanical/overuse factors — prolonged standing, running, obesity, poor footwear and a tight calf/Achilles — predispose to plantar fasciitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.question: How does a night splint help in plantar fasciitis?
options: It immobilises the ankle to prevent all movement
It holds the ankle dorsiflexed overnight to keep the fascia/calf stretched
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.answer: It holds the ankle dorsiflexed overnight to keep the fascia/calf stretched
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Foot & Ankle D.explanation: A night splint holds the ankle in dorsiflexion overnight, maintaining a stretch on the plantar fascia and calf and reducing first-step morning pain.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: A 24-year-old man sustains a closed femoral shaft fracture in a motorbike crash. About 48 hours later he becomes breathless and hypoxic, confused and agitated, and develops a petechial rash over his chest and axillae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: The 24–72h latency after a long-bone fracture with the respiratory + neurological + petechial rash triad is classic fat embolism syndrome.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: What is the characteristic timing of fat embolism syndrome after a long-bone fracture?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: FES classically appears after a latent period of 24–72 hours, which helps distinguish it from immediate post-injury causes.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which fracture pattern most classically precedes fat embolism syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: FES classically follows long-bone (femur/tibia) and pelvic fractures, especially multiple or closed fractures.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which component of the fat embolism triad is usually the earliest and commonest presenting feature?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Respiratory involvement (tachycardia, dyspnoea, hypoxia → ARDS-like picture) is the earliest and commonest feature and the usual presenting problem.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which is considered the MOST SPECIFIC clinical sign of fat embolism syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: The petechial rash (from dermal capillary embolisation → RBC extravasation) is the most specific sign, though it occurs in only ~20–50% of cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Where is the petechial rash of fat embolism syndrome classically distributed?
options: The upper body/trunk, axillae and conjunctivae
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: The upper body/trunk, axillae and conjunctivae
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: The FES petechial rash is classically over the upper trunk, axillae and conjunctivae.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: A patient with a femoral fracture develops respiratory distress and the CTPA is reported as normal. How should this be interpreted regarding fat embolism syndrome?
options: A normal CTPA does NOT exclude FES because the emboli are tiny and distal
FES can only be diagnosed on CTPA
The patient cannot have FES without a filling defect
CTPA is the gold-standard test for FES
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: A normal CTPA does NOT exclude FES because the emboli are tiny and distal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Fat emboli are tiny and lodge distally, so CTPA is often normal — a normal CTPA does not exclude FES, which is a clinical diagnosis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: How is fat embolism syndrome diagnosed?
options: Clinically — from the triad, timing and fracture history (e.g. Gurd's criteria)
By a specific blood test for fat globules
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: Clinically — from the triad, timing and fracture history (e.g. Gurd's criteria)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: FES is a clinical diagnosis based on the triad, timing and fracture history (often using Gurd's criteria); investigations are supportive, and normal imaging does not exclude it.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which arterial blood gas finding is the key supportive feature in fat embolism syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Hypoxia on ABG is the key supportive finding in FES.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: What is the single most important measure to PREVENT fat embolism syndrome after a long-bone fracture?
options: Prompt (early) surgical fixation of the fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: Prompt (early) surgical fixation of the fracture
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Early fixation of long-bone fractures reduces embolisation from the fracture site and is the key preventive measure (with DVT prophylaxis).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: What is the mainstay of treatment for established fat embolism syndrome?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: There is no specific cure; management is supportive — oxygen/respiratory support, ventilation/ICU if severe, IV fluids and monitoring.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: How does fat embolism syndrome typically differ from a pulmonary embolism due to DVT?
options: FES occurs 24–72h post-fracture with a petechial rash and neurological features, whereas PE occurs later with no rash/neuro and a positive CTPA
FES occurs later than PE and has no rash
PE always causes a petechial rash
FES has a raised D-dimer that is diagnostic
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: FES occurs 24–72h post-fracture with a petechial rash and neurological features, whereas PE occurs later with no rash/neuro and a positive CTPA
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: FES presents 24–72h after fracture with the respiratory/neurological/petechial triad; PE tends to occur later (days–weeks), lacks the rash and neuro features, and is confirmed on CTPA.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which fundoscopic findings may be seen in fat embolism syndrome?
options: Retinal haemorrhages and intra-arterial fat globules (Purtscher's-like retinopathy)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: Retinal haemorrhages and intra-arterial fat globules (Purtscher's-like retinopathy)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Fundoscopy may show retinal haemorrhages and intra-arterial fat globules — a Purtscher's-like retinopathy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which full blood count abnormalities are recognised in fat embolism syndrome?
options: A normal FBC is required for diagnosis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Anaemia and thrombocytopenia are recognised in FES (fat globules in urine/sputum may occur but are non-specific).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: What is the typical prognosis of fat embolism syndrome?
options: Most cases are self-limiting and resolve with supportive care within about a week
It always causes permanent brain damage
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: Most cases are self-limiting and resolve with supportive care within about a week
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Most cases are self-limiting and resolve with supportive care (usually within ~1 week); only a minority progress to severe respiratory or cerebral failure.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Through which route can fat emboli reach the brain and skin after first reaching the lungs?
options: Right-to-left shunts or a patent foramen ovale
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: Right-to-left shunts or a patent foramen ovale
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: Fat emboli reach the lungs first, then travel to the brain and skin via shunts or a patent foramen ovale.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: Which statement about the CXR in fat embolism syndrome is correct?
options: It may show bilateral infiltrates (ARDS pattern) or be normal
It always shows a wedge-shaped infarct
It is diagnostic when it shows a pleural effusion
It shows lobar consolidation in all cases
It reliably excludes FES if normal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: It may show bilateral infiltrates (ARDS pattern) or be normal
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: The CXR in FES may show bilateral infiltrates (an ARDS pattern) or be entirely normal, so it is neither sensitive nor specific.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.question: What is the primary pulmonary consequence of fat embolism syndrome?
options: A large central pulmonary artery occlusion
An ARDS-like picture from small-vessel occlusion and free-fatty-acid inflammation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.answer: An ARDS-like picture from small-vessel occlusion and free-fatty-acid inflammation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Fat Embolism S.explanation: In the lungs, small-vessel occlusion plus free-fatty-acid-driven endothelial inflammation produce a contusion/ARDS-like picture — hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: A 45-year-old keen tennis player complains of lateral elbow pain that worsens when gripping and lifting a kettle. Examination reproduces the pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Lateral epicondyle pain reproduced by resisted wrist extension is lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) — overuse of the wrist extensors (ECRB).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which muscle/tendon is most commonly implicated in lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow)?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) is the tendon most commonly implicated in tennis elbow.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: A golfer presents with medial elbow pain that is worst on resisted wrist flexion and pronation. Which diagnosis fits best?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Medial epicondyle pain worse on wrist flexion and pronation is medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) — overuse of the flexor/pronator origin.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Despite the suffix '-itis', what is the true underlying pathology of epicondylitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: A degenerative tendinopathy (not primarily inflammatory)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Epicondylitis is a degenerative tendinopathy of the common tendon origin, not a true inflammatory process, despite its name.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: In a patient with medial epicondylitis, which nerve should be specifically assessed and why?
options: The radial nerve, which winds around the humerus
The ulnar nerve, which runs behind the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel)
The median nerve at the wrist
The axillary nerve at the shoulder
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: The ulnar nerve, which runs behind the medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle through the cubital tunnel, so it can be irritated in medial epicondylitis — check for ulnar symptoms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which mnemonic correctly links golfer's elbow to its site?
options: 'Golf is a LATeral game' — lateral epicondyle
'Golf is a MEDiocre sport' — medial epicondyle
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: 'Golf is a MEDiocre sport' — medial epicondyle
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: 'Golf is a MEDiocre sport' reminds you that golfer's elbow is at the MEDial epicondyle (flexor/pronator origin).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which provocation test suggests LATERAL epicondylitis?
options: Pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension (Cozen's test)
Pain on resisted wrist flexion and pronation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension (Cozen's test)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Cozen's test — pain over the lateral epicondyle on resisted wrist extension (elbow extended) — supports lateral epicondylitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: How is epicondylitis usually diagnosed?
options: MRI of the elbow in all cases
Clinically — localised epicondyle tenderness plus a positive provocation test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Clinically — localised epicondyle tenderness plus a positive provocation test
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Epicondylitis is a clinical diagnosis; imaging (ultrasound/MRI) is reserved for unclear or refractory cases.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which is the single most important ACTIVE treatment for epicondylitis?
options: Physiotherapy with eccentric strengthening and stretching
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Physiotherapy with eccentric strengthening and stretching
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Physiotherapy — eccentric forearm strengthening and stretching — is the key active treatment for epicondylitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: What is the typical natural history of epicondylitis?
options: Self-limiting in most, though it can be slow to resolve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Self-limiting in most, though it can be slow to resolve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Epicondylitis is generally self-limiting, though recovery can be slow (months, sometimes longer); management is conservative.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: How does a counterforce brace (epicondylitis clasp) help in epicondylitis?
options: It offloads the tendon origin by transmitting forces distal to the insertion
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: It offloads the tendon origin by transmitting forces distal to the insertion
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: A counterforce brace/clasp offloads the affected tendon origin by shifting load distal to the insertion, reducing strain on the degenerate tendon.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: A patient with refractory lateral epicondylitis asks about a corticosteroid injection. What is the best advice?
options: It gives short-term relief but may be worse in the long term than conservative treatment
It should be repeated monthly indefinitely
It is contraindicated in all patients
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: It gives short-term relief but may be worse in the long term than conservative treatment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Steroid injections provide short-term relief but are associated with possibly worse long-term outcomes, so they are reserved for refractory cases and used sparingly.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: On examination, a patient has lateral elbow pain reproduced by resisted extension of the middle finger. Which test is this, and what does it suggest?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Maudsley's test — lateral epicondylitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Maudsley's test (resisted middle-finger extension reproducing lateral epicondyle pain) supports lateral epicondylitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which differential should particularly be considered in a patient with 'lateral epicondylitis' that fails to respond, with pain more distal over the forearm?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Radial tunnel syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Radial tunnel syndrome is a differential for refractory/atypical lateral elbow pain (posterior interosseous nerve compression), with tenderness more distal than the epicondyle.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which movement most specifically provokes the pain of MEDIAL epicondylitis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Resisted wrist flexion and pronation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Medial epicondylitis pain is provoked by wrist flexion and pronation — the actions of the flexor/pronator group that originates at the medial epicondyle.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: What clinical features are common to BOTH tennis and golfer's elbow?
options: Fever and a hot swollen joint
A locked elbow with mechanical block
Night pain relieved by shaking the hand
Epicondyle pain and tenderness radiating down the forearm with a weak grip
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Epicondyle pain and tenderness radiating down the forearm with a weak grip
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Both give localised epicondyle pain/tenderness radiating down the forearm with a weak grip; they differ in which epicondyle and which provoking movement.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which statement about the relative frequency of the two forms of epicondylitis is correct?
options: Tennis elbow (lateral) is the commoner of the two
Golfer's elbow is far commoner than tennis elbow
They occur with exactly equal frequency
Both are rare and mainly paediatric
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Tennis elbow (lateral) is the commoner of the two
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) is the commoner of the two forms.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: A middle-aged office worker who does a lot of repetitive keyboard and mouse work develops lateral elbow pain over several weeks with no trauma. What is the most likely underlying process?
options: A stress fracture of the radial head
An overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: An overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Repetitive forearm use causing gradual lateral elbow pain is an overuse tendinopathy of the common extensor origin — occupational tennis elbow (not just athletes).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which of the following is the LEAST appropriate first-line management for newly diagnosed epicondylitis?
options: Activity modification and avoiding provoking movements
Reassurance that it is usually self-limiting
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Immediate surgical tendon release
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Surgery (tendon release) is a last resort for refractory cases; first-line management is conservative — rest/activity modification, analgesia, reassurance and physiotherapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: A patient with medial elbow pain also reports tingling in the little and ring fingers. What does this additional feature suggest?
options: Ulnar nerve irritation at the cubital tunnel accompanying the medial epicondylitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Ulnar nerve irritation at the cubital tunnel accompanying the medial epicondylitis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Little/ring finger tingling points to ulnar nerve irritation at the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, which can accompany golfer's elbow — always assess the ulnar nerve in medial epicondylitis.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which of the following best describes the role of imaging in epicondylitis?
options: MRI is required to make the diagnosis
Imaging is not routinely needed; ultrasound or MRI is reserved for unclear or refractory cases
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: Imaging is not routinely needed; ultrasound or MRI is reserved for unclear or refractory cases
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: Epicondylitis is a clinical diagnosis; ultrasound or MRI is used only when the diagnosis is unclear or the condition is refractory.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.question: Which forearm muscle group originates at the medial epicondyle and is overused in golfer's elbow?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.answer: The wrist flexors and pronators
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Epicondylitis.explanation: The common flexor origin (wrist flexors and pronators) arises from the medial epicondyle and is overused in golfer's elbow; the extensor/supinator origin arises from the lateral epicondyle.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A 22-year-old man falls onto an outstretched hand playing rugby. He holds his arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, and the normal rounded contour of the shoulder is lost (squared shoulder). What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Anterior shoulder dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: FOOSH with the arm abducted/externally rotated and a squared-off shoulder (lost deltoid contour) is a classic anterior glenohumeral dislocation — the commonest direction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which nerve is most commonly injured in an anterior shoulder dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Axillary nerve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The axillary nerve is at risk in anterior dislocation, causing weak deltoid and sensory loss over the 'regimental badge' area.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: How would you test for an axillary nerve injury after a shoulder dislocation?
options: Test wrist extension and sensation over the anatomical snuffbox
Test thumb opposition and thenar sensation
Test deltoid power (abduction) and sensation over the 'regimental badge' (lateral deltoid)
Test finger abduction and little-finger sensation
Test elbow flexion and forearm sensation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Test deltoid power (abduction) and sensation over the 'regimental badge' (lateral deltoid)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The axillary nerve supplies deltoid (abduction) and the skin over the lateral deltoid (regimental badge area) — both are tested to detect its injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A patient dislocates their shoulder during a generalised tonic-clonic seizure. The arm is held adducted and internally rotated and resists external rotation. Which type of dislocation is this, and what is the risk?
options: Posterior — easily missed on the AP X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Posterior — easily missed on the AP X-ray
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Seizures/electric shock cause posterior dislocation (arm adducted, internally rotated, resisting external rotation); it is easily missed on AP and needs an axillary/Y view.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which classic triad of causes should raise suspicion of a POSTERIOR shoulder dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Epilepsy (seizures), electrocution and extreme trauma
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The '3 Es' — Epilepsy, Electrocution and Extreme trauma — classically cause posterior shoulder dislocation via violent internal-rotator contraction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which X-ray view is essential to detect a posterior shoulder dislocation that may look near-normal on the AP film?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: An axillary (or scapular-Y) view
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A posterior dislocation is easily missed on AP; the axillary or scapular-Y view is essential to confirm it (the 'lightbulb' sign is a clue).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is a Hill-Sachs lesion?
options: An impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head
A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: An impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A Hill-Sachs lesion is an impaction fracture of the posterolateral humeral head from anterior dislocation, predisposing to recurrence.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is a Bankart lesion?
options: An impaction fracture of the humeral head
An injury to the anteroinferior glenoid labrum
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: An injury to the anteroinferior glenoid labrum
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A Bankart lesion is injury to the anteroinferior glenoid labrum (± bone), a cause of recurrent anterior instability.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Why is it essential to assess and document neurovascular status BOTH before and after reducing a shoulder dislocation?
options: It is only needed before reduction
It is only needed after reduction
Neurovascular injury never occurs in the shoulder
Reduction itself can injure the axillary nerve, so pre- and post-reduction findings must both be recorded
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Reduction itself can injure the axillary nerve, so pre- and post-reduction findings must both be recorded
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Reduction can itself injure the axillary nerve; documenting status before and after is clinically and medicolegally essential.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Why is sedation or analgesia given before attempting closed reduction of a shoulder dislocation?
options: To relax the rotator cuff muscle spasm that otherwise prevents reduction
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: To relax the rotator cuff muscle spasm that otherwise prevents reduction
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Muscle (rotator cuff) spasm blocks reduction; sedation/analgesia relaxes the muscles to allow gentle, controlled reduction and avoid fracture/nerve injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: After successful closed reduction of an anterior shoulder dislocation, what are the immediate next steps?
options: Apply a plaster cast for 6 weeks
Arrange urgent open surgery for all patients
Re-assess neurovascular status and obtain a post-reduction X-ray, then immobilise in a sling
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Re-assess neurovascular status and obtain a post-reduction X-ray, then immobilise in a sling
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Post-reduction, re-check neurovascular status, confirm relocation (and no iatrogenic fracture) on X-ray, then immobilise in a sling followed by physiotherapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A 19-year-old has had three anterior shoulder dislocations in a year, with an MRI showing a Bankart lesion. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Surgical stabilisation (e.g. Bankart repair)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Recurrent instability — especially in young patients with a Bankart/Hill-Sachs lesion — is treated with surgical stabilisation such as a Bankart repair.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which joint is the most commonly dislocated major joint in the body?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The shoulder (glenohumeral)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The glenohumeral joint has a shallow socket and huge range — highly mobile but unstable — making it the most commonly dislocated major joint.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A high-energy road traffic collision leaves a patient with a grossly deformed knee that spontaneously relocated at the scene. Which structure most urgently needs assessment?
options: The popliteal artery (distal pulses / ankle-brachial index)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The popliteal artery (distal pulses / ankle-brachial index)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Knee (tibiofemoral) dislocation is limb-threatening due to popliteal artery injury — assess distal pulses/ABI with a low threshold for CT angiography, even after spontaneous reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A patient sustains a posterior hip dislocation in a dashboard injury. Besides sciatic nerve injury, what is the key late complication of delayed reduction?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Delayed reduction of a hip dislocation risks avascular necrosis of the femoral head, so prompt reduction is essential.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: In a posterior hip dislocation, how is the affected leg classically positioned?
options: Shortened and externally rotated (as in NOF fracture)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Flexed, adducted and internally rotated
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A posterior hip dislocation classically holds the leg flexed, adducted and internally rotated (contrast the shortened, externally rotated leg of a hip fracture).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which nerve and which artery are principally at risk in an elbow dislocation?
options: Median/ulnar nerves and the brachial artery
Common peroneal nerve and popliteal artery
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Median/ulnar nerves and the brachial artery
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Elbow dislocation (usually posterior, from FOOSH) risks the brachial artery and the median/ulnar nerves, plus associated fractures ('terrible triad').

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which patient group is at highest risk of RECURRENT shoulder dislocation after a first anterior dislocation?
options: Young patients (and those with Bankart/Hill-Sachs lesions)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Young patients (and those with Bankart/Hill-Sachs lesions)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Younger patients — and those with structural Bankart/Hill-Sachs lesions — have the highest recurrence risk, often warranting surgical stabilisation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: An older patient continues to have shoulder weakness and pain after a reduced anterior dislocation, with normal X-rays. Which associated injury should be suspected?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: A rotator cuff tear
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Rotator cuff tears commonly accompany shoulder dislocation in older patients and should be suspected with persistent weakness/pain despite a normal post-reduction X-ray.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the correct first principle when a patient presents with any acute joint dislocation?
options: Assess and document distal neurovascular status, then image and reduce promptly
Apply ice and review in clinic in a week
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Assess and document distal neurovascular status, then image and reduce promptly
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: For any dislocation: assess/document neurovascular status before (and after) reduction, image to confirm direction/fracture, and reduce promptly.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: On the AP shoulder X-ray of a posterior dislocation, the humeral head classically appears rounded and symmetrical. What is this sign called?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The 'lightbulb' (ice-cream-cone) sign
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: In posterior dislocation the internally rotated humeral head looks like a symmetrical 'lightbulb' on the AP film — a subtle clue prompting an axillary/Y view.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A patient with an anterior shoulder dislocation cannot abduct the arm and has numbness over the lateral aspect of the upper arm after reduction. What has most likely happened?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: An axillary nerve injury
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Weak abduction (deltoid) plus sensory loss over the lateral deltoid/'regimental badge' after dislocation or reduction indicates an axillary nerve injury.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A restrained front-seat passenger in a high-speed car crash has severe hip pain. The right leg is shortened, adducted and internally rotated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Posterior hip dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A shortened, adducted, internally rotated leg ('everything IN') after a dashboard injury is a posterior hip dislocation — the commonest type (~90%).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Why does the hip require major force to dislocate, unlike the shoulder?
options: The hip is a deep, stable ball-and-socket joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The hip is a deep, stable ball-and-socket joint
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The hip is a deep, congruent, stable ball-and-socket joint, so it takes high-energy trauma (e.g. a dashboard injury) to dislocate it.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which nerve is classically at risk in a POSTERIOR hip dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Sciatic nerve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Posterior hip dislocation risks the sciatic nerve, classically producing a foot drop via common peroneal nerve damage.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: How does a sciatic nerve injury from a posterior hip dislocation typically present?
options: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and altered sensation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Foot drop with weak dorsiflexion and altered sensation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Sciatic nerve injury (commonly its common peroneal division) causes foot drop — weak ankle dorsiflexion and sensory loss — so document dorsiflexion and sensation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the leg position in an ANTERIOR hip dislocation?
options: Abducted and externally rotated, with no shortening
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Abducted and externally rotated, with no shortening
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Anterior hip dislocation holds the leg abducted and externally rotated with no shortening — 'everything goes OUT'.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the single most important reason to reduce a hip dislocation urgently (within ~4–6 hours)?
options: To reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: To reduce the risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The femoral head has a precarious retrograde blood supply; the longer it is dislocated, the higher the risk of avascular necrosis — so reduce fast.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the classic mechanism of a posterior hip dislocation?
options: A direct blow to the greater trochanter
A 'dashboard injury' — axial force through a flexed hip and knee
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: A 'dashboard injury' — axial force through a flexed hip and knee
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Axial force transmitted through a flexed hip and knee (knee striking the dashboard) drives the femoral head posteriorly out of the acetabulum.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which imaging is used AFTER reduction of a hip dislocation to detect associated acetabular/femoral head fractures and intra-articular fragments?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: CT
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: CT is often obtained after reduction to assess associated acetabular/femoral head fractures and any trapped intra-articular fragments.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A hip dislocation is a high-energy injury. What is the correct initial approach on arrival?
options: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient follow-up
Apply skin traction and review next day
ABCDE trauma assessment and analgesia, looking for associated injuries
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: ABCDE trauma assessment and analgesia, looking for associated injuries
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: It is a trauma patient — begin with ABCDE and analgesia, assess neurovascular status, and look for associated injuries before urgent reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which memory hook fits a posterior hip dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: 'Everything goes IN' (adducted, internally rotated, shortened)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Posterior dislocation = shortened, adducted, internally rotated — 'everything goes IN to the box'.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: After successful reduction of a hip dislocation, which steps are appropriate?
options: Apply a hip spica cast for 3 months
Re-assess neurovascular status, obtain a post-reduction X-ray/CT, then protected weight-bearing and physiotherapy
Arrange total hip replacement for all patients
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Re-assess neurovascular status, obtain a post-reduction X-ray/CT, then protected weight-bearing and physiotherapy
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Post-reduction: re-check neurovascular status, confirm a congruent joint on X-ray/CT, then protected weight-bearing and physiotherapy.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the definitive management if closed reduction of a hip dislocation fails or there is an incarcerated bony fragment?
options: Immediate total hip replacement in all
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Open reduction
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Open reduction is indicated when closed reduction fails or an incarcerated fragment/associated fracture blocks a congruent reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which nerve and vessels are principally at risk in an ANTERIOR hip dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Femoral nerve and femoral vessels
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Anterior dislocation risks the femoral nerve and femoral vessels — assess quadriceps/knee jerk and distal pulses.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which of the following is a recognised late complication of a hip dislocation besides avascular necrosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Secondary (post-traumatic) osteoarthritis
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Secondary/post-traumatic osteoarthritis is a recognised late complication, along with recurrent dislocation and heterotopic ossification.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A patient has a posterior hip dislocation reduced 8 hours after injury. Months later they develop worsening hip pain; an X-ray shows femoral head collapse. What is the diagnosis?
options: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Delayed reduction predisposes to avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which can present later with pain and femoral head collapse.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Why is it essential to document neurovascular status BOTH before and after reducing a hip dislocation?
options: Neurovascular injury never occurs at the hip
Reduction can itself injure the sciatic/femoral nerve, so pre- and post-reduction findings must both be recorded
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Reduction can itself injure the sciatic/femoral nerve, so pre- and post-reduction findings must both be recorded
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Reduction can injure the sciatic (posterior) or femoral (anterior) nerve; documenting status before and after is essential clinically and medicolegally.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A 30-year-old falls onto an outstretched hand and presents with a painful, swollen, deformed elbow held in flexion, with a prominent olecranon posteriorly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Posterior elbow dislocation
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: FOOSH with a painful, deformed elbow held flexed and a prominent olecranon is a posterior elbow dislocation — ~90% of elbow dislocations.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: The elbow is the second most commonly dislocated major joint in adults. Which joint is first?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The shoulder
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The shoulder is the commonest dislocated major joint; the elbow is second in adults (and the commonest dislocation in children).

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What defines a COMPLEX (as opposed to simple) elbow dislocation?
options: There is an associated fracture (e.g. radial head, coronoid, olecranon), making it unstable
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: There is an associated fracture (e.g. radial head, coronoid, olecranon), making it unstable
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A complex elbow dislocation is a fracture-dislocation (radial head/coronoid/olecranon), often unstable and frequently requiring surgery — unlike a simple ligamentous dislocation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which combination of injuries constitutes the elbow 'terrible triad'?
options: Dislocation + ulnar shaft + radial shaft fractures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Dislocation + radial head + coronoid fractures
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The 'terrible triad' is elbow dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures — an unstable pattern usually needing surgical fixation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which artery must be specifically assessed (distal pulse, perfusion) before and after reducing an elbow dislocation?
options: The radial artery at the wrist only
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The brachial artery
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The brachial artery crosses the elbow and can be injured; assess the distal radial pulse, capillary refill and hand perfusion before and after reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A patient with an elbow dislocation has an absent radial pulse and a progressively worsening neurological deficit in the hand. What does this represent?
options: An indication for a sling only
A surgical emergency requiring urgent exploration/vascular assessment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: A surgical emergency requiring urgent exploration/vascular assessment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: An absent pulse or progressive deficit signals vascular/nerve injury — a surgical emergency needing urgent intervention.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which nerve is especially vulnerable at the elbow and should be tested (intrinsic hand muscles, medial 1½ fingers) after dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Ulnar nerve
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: The ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle and is especially vulnerable at the elbow — test intrinsic hand muscles and medial 1½ finger sensation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What complication of an elbow injury is signalled by pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch of the forearm?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Forearm compartment syndrome
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch suggest forearm compartment syndrome — a limb-threatening emergency, especially with vascular compromise/tight swelling.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Why should X-rays be taken both before and after reduction of an elbow dislocation?
options: Pre-reduction confirms the direction and any associated fractures (simple vs complex); post-reduction confirms a congruent, concentric relocation with no trapped fragment
To measure the carrying angle only
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Pre-reduction confirms the direction and any associated fractures (simple vs complex); post-reduction confirms a congruent, concentric relocation with no trapped fragment
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Pre-reduction films confirm direction and associated fractures (simple vs complex); post-reduction films confirm a concentric relocation without a trapped fragment.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: What is the correct management principle for a SIMPLE elbow dislocation after reduction?
options: Brief immobilisation then EARLY mobilisation to avoid stiffness
No immobilisation and immediate heavy lifting
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Brief immobilisation then EARLY mobilisation to avoid stiffness
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A simple dislocation is reduced then only briefly immobilised, with early mobilisation, because the elbow is very prone to stiffness/contracture.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which is the COMMONEST complication after an elbow dislocation?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Stiffness / loss of extension
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Loss of extension/stiffness is the commonest complication, which is why early mobilisation is emphasised after reduction.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A 3-year-old is brought in after being pulled up by the arm; she holds the arm pronated and refuses to use it, with no swelling or deformity. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Pulled elbow (radial head subluxation)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: A low-energy longitudinal pull on a young child's arm causing radial head subluxation is a 'pulled elbow' — distinct from a true elbow dislocation.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A complex elbow fracture-dislocation with an incongruent joint is identified. What is the appropriate management?
options: Closed reduction and early movement alone
Open reduction ± internal fixation / ligament repair
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Open reduction ± internal fixation / ligament repair
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Fracture-dislocations, gross instability, an irreducible/incongruent joint or vascular injury need surgery — open reduction ± internal fixation/ligament (or vascular) repair.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which set of associated fractures should be actively sought on the pre-reduction X-ray of an elbow dislocation?
options: Radial head, coronoid and olecranon (and medial epicondyle in children)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: Radial head, coronoid and olecranon (and medial epicondyle in children)
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: Associated radial head, coronoid, olecranon (and paediatric medial epicondyle) fractures define a complex dislocation and change management towards surgery.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: Which bony landmark relationship is disrupted in a posterior elbow dislocation?
options: The normal equilateral triangle of the olecranon and the two epicondyles
The radiocapitellar line at the wrist
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The normal equilateral triangle of the olecranon and the two epicondyles
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.explanation: In a posterior elbow dislocation the prominent olecranon disrupts the normal equilateral triangle formed by the olecranon and the medial and lateral epicondyles.

conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.question: A 25-year-old is brought in after a high-speed car crash with a grossly deformed, unstable knee. After urgent reduction, which structure is the priority to assess and re-assess?
conditions__ORTHOPAEDICS__Dislocations.answer: The popliteal artery
